1923c855d73f3ef3: WASHINGTON: US vice-president JD Vance posted on X Saturday blaming immigration for violence during protests in France, while sharing a video showing the city hall in Limoges on fire.

"Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility. They were told it would lead to this and they didn't listen," Vance wrote on X.
"I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn," he added.

Vance, who is seen as a potential presidential candidate in the 2028 election, also drew a connection to upcoming midterm races for congressional seats on Nov 3, where Republicans are not expected to perform well.
"And I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country," Vance said.
Major protests gripped France on Saturday, where police clashed with demonstrators as nationwide marches against soaring inflation devolved into street violence, widespread looting and fires.
Vance, 42, represents the most nationalist and identitarian wing of the Republican Party, and often criticises Europe's immigration policies, which he considers too lax.
Vance went so far as to lecture Europeans on the subject during a February 2025 speech in Munich.
25bdeb5e7e1b60c0: KUALA LUMPUR: Sikap segelintir penunggang motosikal yang memandang ringan keselamatan diri walaupun berulang kali dinasihati keluarga membimbangkan polis.
Timbalan Ketua Jabatan Siasatan dan Penguatkuasaan Trafik Kuala Lumpur, Suffian Abdullah, berkata sikap itu bukan sahaja membahayakan penunggang, malah pengguna jalan raya lain.
“Hampir 90% kesalahan dikesan melibatkan motosikal yang tidak sempurna atau penunggang tidak mempunyai lesen memandu sah.

“Antara kesalahan dikenal pasti ialah pengubahsuaian komponen motosikal termasuk brek dan ekzos. Remaja bawah umur juga kerap dikesan, namun saringan masih dijalankan untuk menentukan jumlah sebenar mereka yang ditahan,” katanya.

Beliau berkata demikian selepas operasi bersepadu yang menyaksikan polis memeriksa kira-kira 800 motosikal, menyita 60 daripadanya dan mengeluarkan kira-kira 300 saman atas pelbagai kesalahan trafik di ibu negara, awal pagi tadi.

Operasi bagi membanteras kesalahan trafik dan samseng jalanan itu membabitkan 80 pegawai dan anggota polis, dengan bantuan 12 anggota Jabatan Pengangkutan Jalan serta lima Agensi Antidadah Kebangsaan.
Suffian menggesa ibu bapa dan penjaga memantau pergerakan anak-anak serta memastikan mereka tidak menunggang motosikal tanpa lesen sah.
2a31b10cdc97982e: PETALING JAYA: Seizing the assets of traffic offenders to compensate accident victims will not, on its own, reduce road fatalities, says a road safety expert, who called for stronger enforcement and better road infrastructure.

On Oct 15, transport minister Loke Siew Fook said the government was considering seizing the assets of traffic offenders convicted of serious offences to compensate road accident victims and their families, particularly when offenders could not afford to pay.
Universiti Putra Malaysia’s Law Teik Hua said asset seizures might have a financial deterrent effect but would not necessarily change driving behaviour or bring down road deaths.

He said the government should prioritise sustained enforcement against offences such as driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, speeding and running red lights, as well as strengthen the Kejara demerit points system.
“The government should not rely solely on severe penalties,” he told FMT.
“The causes of accidents must be addressed comprehensively, including through safer road design, measures to tackle high-risk locations, and automated enforcement."

To ensure victims and their families were not left waiting for compensation while the offenders’ assets were being sold, Law proposed that the government establish an interim compensation fund and recover the money from offenders through legal channels.
Universiti Malaya criminologist Haezreena Begum Abdul Hamid said any asset seizure must have a clear legal basis and protect the rights of innocent family members.

“We cannot arbitrarily seize the assets of a spouse or innocent family members simply because they are related to an offender,” she said, adding that financial penalties alone would not reduce traffic offences without consistent law enforcement.
6a06bf3b22c65dbe: WASHINGTON: Carrying an umbrella painted with the words "vote, power, people," retired teacher Sabine Carlson said the lesson plan for Saturday's "No Kings" marches was clear.
"It's great to voice your anger, and we have long lists of complaints, but the most important thing of all is to go and vote," the 66-year-old Democrat from Washington's suburbs told AFP.
At the demonstration near the country's Capitol, Carlson joined one of the estimated 3,000 events organised by the prominent anti-Trump movement across the United States on Saturday.

Rather than holding massive marches, the latest "No Kings" events varied across the country -- with honking convoys, concerts and neighborhood gatherings. It was the fourth iteration of the demonstrations since US President Donald Trump returned to office.
The stated goal of the event was to fire up voters just as Americans begin casting ballots in the midterm elections, where majority Republicans face fierce opposition.
Democrats are seeking to take control of Congress by campaigning on cost of living issues and an unpopular war in the Middle East.
Focused on early voting ahead of election day on Nov 3, the events ranged from New York to Los Angeles and other blue stronghold cities, to small towns across the nation.

"I think it's one of the most important votes that is coming up, and it's really important to make people aware, and also make sure they know where to look up the procedures and make sure they're registered correctly," Carlson said.
"Don't go to the wrong polling station."
'An act of joy'
Most areas of the US allow voters to cast their ballots ahead of time, sometimes weeks in advance.

Alma Couverthie, who oversees grassroots organising efforts for democracy watchdog Common Cause, said the point of the "No Kings" rallies was "reclaiming voting for what it truly is: an act of power, an act of service, and an act of joy."

Trump has openly criticised the practice of mail-in voting, and opponents have expressed concern that the administration will attempt to undermine the results -- especially if Republicans end up losing, as opinion polls show is likely.
By advocating for voting early, "No Kings" organisers hope to cut off the potential for any malfeasance.

"The best way to prevent any funny business from this administration after election day is to make sure that our turnout is massive, so clear and so overwhelming that our victory for democracy is impossible to question," Couverthie said.
'We want our country back'
One 52-year-old military veteran who joined Saturday's protest did so seeking catharsis from the current state of American politics.
"I am so disillusioned by what I thought I was serving versus what this country has become," the Virginia resident told AFP, declining to give his name.
"Over the last 18 months -- I finally came to this conclusion about six months ago -- I've been mourning my country."
Carrying an umbrella with the message "Vote for humanity. End this circus now. We want our country back," he said he hoped to see "a robust response come Nov 3 from the American people."
Beyond Washington, likeminded Americans echoed his hopes and fears.
Outside a church in Gastonia, North Carolina, women carried signs that read "Honk for Democracy" and "Make a plan to vote!"

In Portland, Maine, demonstrators bundled up against the autumn chill waved the American flag and carried signs reading "Your Vote is Your Voice" and "No Kings, No Cowards Collins," in reference to Republican incumbent Senator Susan Collins, who faces a tough re-election race.
In Wilton Manors, Florida, demonstrators spent the sunny day sporting shorts and sunglasses, carrying signs reading "Enough is enough."
"Trump is destroying America" and "Democracy not Autocracy," some signs read in Atlanta, Georgia.
A man dressed as Uncle Sam at a protest in Kansas City, Missouri stood near a sign reading "Uncle Sam Says Make American What Was Promised."

In Houston, a large crowd marched through city streets carrying a banner that read "Resist All Corruption" and handmade signs reading "War Crimes Don't Hide Sex Crimes" and "Rein in the Mad King Vote Blue."

All across California -- from San Diego to San Francisco and many points beyond -- crowds filled the streets, including in Los Angeles, where protesters marched to city hall carrying signs declaring "No Kings", and at least one that added "No Idiots Either".
c069610256eabc2b: PETALING JAYA: Universiti perlu memperluas kursus jangka pendek penjagaan warga emas bagi melahirkan lebih ramai penjaga terlatih menjelang Malaysia menjadi negara tua pada 2048, kata Ketua Pegawai Eksekutif Agensi Kelayakan Malaysia (MQA), Mohammad Shatar Sabran.
Beliau berkata, kursus yang disahkan dari segi kualiti itu boleh membantu anak-anak menjaga ibu bapa, selain membuka peluang kepada peserta menawarkan khidmat penjagaan secara sambilan.

“Saya di MQA apa yang telah saya pesan kepada semua universiti adalah menawarkan kursus jangka pendek untuk penjagaan warga tua dan kursus-kursus ini mempunyai verifikasi kualiti,” katanya kepada FMT.
Beliau berkata, peserta yang menamatkan kursus dan memperoleh sijil boleh diberikan kepercayaan untuk menjaga warga emas, sekali gus membantu keluarga yang memerlukan khidmat berkenaan.
Shatar yang juga pakar sosial berkata, model penjagaan mengikut jam seperti yang ditawarkan bagi kanak-kanak juga boleh diterapkan untuk warga emas, mengikut keperluan keluarga.
Katanya, beberapa universiti sudah menawarkan kursus sedemikian, namun pelaksanaannya masih belum meluas dan perlu diperluas bagi memenuhi permintaan.

Pada 5 Okt lalu, Menteri Ekonomi, Akmal Nasrullah Nasir berkata, Malaysia hanya mempunyai tempoh kira-kira 27 tahun untuk membuat persiapan menyeluruh bagi menghadapi status negara tua menjelang 2048, iaitu fasa peralihan jauh lebih pantas berbanding beberapa negara maju.

Katanya, tempoh singkat itu memberi ruang masa terhad kepada kerajaan untuk memperkukuh kesiapsiagaan negara berbanding Perancis yang mengambil 115 tahun, Australia (73 tahun) dan Amerika Syarikat (69 tahun).

Sementara itu, mengulas cadangan NGO Pusat Sumber untuk Kemajuan Masyarakat dan Perumahan (Reach) supaya kerajaan memberi pelepasan cukai pendapatan kepada anak menanggung bayaran sewa atau ansuran pinjaman perumahan ibu bapa bagi meringankan beban kewangan mereka, Shatar berkata insentif tersebut boleh menggalakkan anak mengambil tanggungjawab terhadap kebajikan golongan terbabit, mengeratkan hubungan kekeluargaan dan mengurangkan risiko pengabaian warga emas termasuk kes kematian senyap.

“Kalau hubungan baik dan anak sentiasa mengambil tanggungjawab, mereka akan sentiasa memantau ibu bapa. Sekurang-kurangnya, risiko kes seperti kematian senyap dapat dikurangkan walaupun kita mungkin tidak dapat menghapuskannya secara keseluruhan,” katanya.
Pada 14 Okt lalu, Ketua Penyelaras Reach, Iskandar Samad, berkata cadangan itu selaras usaha kerajaan memperkukuh kebajikan warga emas susulan pengumuman Belanjawan 2027.
Perdana Menteri, Anwar Ibrahim, ketika membentangkan belanjawan itu pada 9 Okt lalu mengumumkan peruntukan RM1.3 bilion bagi bantuan warga emas yang dijangka memanfaatkan hampir 200,000 penerima.
Bagaimanapun, Shatar menegaskan penjagaan warga emas tidak boleh diserahkan sepenuhnya kepada kerajaan, sebaliknya memerlukan kerjasama keluarga, NGO dan masyarakat.
Katanya, kegagalan menyediakan penjagaan sewajarnya juga boleh meningkatkan beban kewangan kerajaan, termasuk kos berkaitan pengurusan kes kematian senyap dan penjagaan di pusat jagaan.
d1e4dbec7bb188c4: PETALING JAYA: An MP has questioned the Kuala Lumpur immigration department's intention to investigate alleged irregularities in the issuance of special passes at its office, saying the allegations could involve a senior officer.

Kepong MP Lim Lip Eng said the immigration department headquarters should take over the investigation, while allegations of corruption and wrongdoing should be referred to the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission and the police.
Yesterday, Kuala Lumpur immigration director Hamsha Injau said the department’s integrity division would conduct an investigation to determine if the allegations, raised by a news portal, were true.
He said no misconduct would be tolerated, and appropriate action would be taken if there was evidence of any breach of the law or regulations.

Malaysiakini had reported that special passes, which were intended to assist foreign nationals facing emergencies or urgent circumstances, were allegedly being systematically abused to extend their stay in Malaysia.

The report also alleged that the operation involved local intermediaries who handled applications, collected applicants’ passports, and sent their photographs to immigration officers through messaging applications for preliminary verification.
In a statement today, Lim said the authorities should not wait for media exposure to provide an explanation.
"The people want to know the actions that have been taken since Aug 10 (when the allegations first surfaced), not just hear another announcement of an investigation," he said.
950bde01c36ecfa0: PETALING JAYA: Cadangan menyita aset pesalah trafik bagi membayar pampasan kepada mangsa nahas perlu dilaksanakan berlandaskan undang-undang dan tidak boleh menjejaskan hak ahli keluarga yang tidak bersalah, kata pakar.
Pakar Kriminologi Universiti Malaya, Haezreena Begum Abdul Hamid, berkata penyitaan aset mesti berlandaskan undang-undang bagi melindungi hak keluarga pesalah yang tidak bersalah.
Katanya, keadilan bukan sekadar memastikan mangsa menerima pampasan tetapi melindungi hak pihak ketiga mengikut garis panduan mahkamah.

“Penyitaan mesti mempunyai asas undang-undang yang jelas. Kita tidak boleh sewenang-wenangnya mengambil aset pasangan atau ahli keluarga yang tidak bersalah hanya kerana mereka mempunyai hubungan dengan pesalah,” katanya kepada FMT.
Beliau berkata, hukuman kewangan semata-mata tidak menjamin pengurangan kesalahan trafik jika tidak disertai penguatkuasaan undang-undang yang konsisten.

Pada 15 Okt lalu, Menteri Pengangkutan, Loke Siew Fook, berkata kerajaan sedang mempertimbangkan cadangan menyita aset pesalah trafik yang disabitkan kesalahan serius bagi membayar pampasan kepada mangsa kemalangan jalan raya dan keluarga mereka.
Katanya, langkah itu antara beberapa pilihan sedang diteliti bagi memastikan mangsa atau keluarga mereka tetap menerima pampasan, khususnya apabila pesalah tidak mampu membuat bayaran.

Sementara itu, Pakar Keselamatan Jalan Raya Universiti Putra Malaysia, Law Teik Hua, berkata penyitaan aset mungkin memberi kesan pencegahan dari sudut kewangan, tetapi tidak mampu mengubah sikap pemandu atau mengurangkan kadar kematian jalan raya secara bersendirian.

Katanya, kerajaan perlu mengutamakan pencegahan melalui penguatkuasaan berterusan terhadap kesalahan seperti memandu bawah pengaruh alkohol atau dadah, memandu laju dan melanggar lampu merah, selain memperkemas Sistem Mata Demerit Kejara.

“Kerajaan tidak seharusnya bergantung pada hukuman berat semata-mata. Punca kemalangan perlu ditangani secara menyeluruh merangkumi reka bentuk jalan raya yang selamat, menangani lokasi berisiko dan penguatkuasaan automatik,” katanya.

Bagi mengelakkan mangsa terbeban sementara menunggu proses penjualan aset selesai, Law mencadangkan kerajaan mewujudkan dana pampasan sementara sebelum mendapatkan semula wang daripada pesalah melalui saluran undang-undang.
4a57d3c28cf22595: I’m not shocked by the revelation that some children are refusing to sit next to their Christian or Muslim classmates. I knew it was coming.
On Oct 15, Puncak Borneo MP Willie Mongin raised concerns in the Dewan Rakyat about religious intolerance among primary school children.
He said a teacher told him that some children said: “I don’t want to sit with them because they eat pork,” or “I don’t want to sit with them because they wear a cross”.

This is far more than a classroom management problem. It is a symptom of a society that is quietly fracturing along ethnic and religious lines — and in Malaysia’s multiethnic reality, that fracture is a national security threat.

In a country where the delicate balance between the Malay-Muslim majority and the Chinese, Indian, and indigenous minorities has historically been the cornerstone of stability, the early crystallisation of “us versus them” at the primary-school level is terribly dangerous, to say the least.

When children are socialised to view difference as a threat rather than a shared reality, the foundation of our society — the mutual accommodation that has kept us together for decades — begins to crumble before critical thinking even develops.
As Mongin warned, if this trend is not addressed at the youngest age, it will inevitably spread, feeding the very 3R controversies that have destabilised Malaysian politics in recent years.
This should not be treated as an isolated case for it reflects deeper structural patterns that threaten Malaysia’s unity.

It is dangerous because it erodes the trust and understanding that underpin social relations, business partnerships and even political alliances. Worse, it creates a radicalisation pipeline: isolated children become vulnerable to extremist online narratives.
I said I knew it was coming. The rise of ethno-religious nationalism, especially since the early 2000s, has amplified our differences.

When an increasing number of politicians unashamedly fire up religion- or race-related issues to win votes or to be seen as champions of their race or religion — and then get away with it or are cheered on by their supporters — what do you expect to happen?
Political rhetoric often frames racial and religious purity as mobilisation tools, and children absorb the tone of such public discourse.
Another reason is that the different communities have moved into their own silos, interacting at work, in school and elsewhere only when and where necessary.

And unlike in the past, the norm today is for children to play or share activities with those of their own race. When school is the only mixed space, and that space is already poisoned by home prejudices or online content, the classroom turns into a battleground instead of a bridge.

Digital poisoning makes the problem worse. Some social media platforms prioritise outrage, with algorithms amplifying hate speech and fake news. Children encounter dehumanising content that normalises rejection of the “other.”
When a pupil says, “I don’t want to sit with them because they wear a cross,” they may have internalised a viral meme or attack on that symbol.
I can go on, but all of us know there are many unspeakable elephants in the room that authorities need to address.
Existing “unity” programmes are well-intentioned but episodic and top-down. They rely on short camps or lectures rather than daily, sustained interaction.

Without structural changes in curriculum and teacher training, they will continue to fail in shifting deep prejudices. Teacher training must include conflict resolution and intercultural communication. Remedies must be structural, not performative as they have been.

Curriculum reform should prioritise critical thinking, media literacy and emotional intelligence over rote “unity” modules. Students need to learn how to deconstruct hate speech and engage in dialogue.
Schools need more group activities to build positive associations.
Digital literacy must become a core subject, not an add-on. Perhaps workshops can be organised for parents on how to guide their children’s online consumption.
Government and civil society must emphasize shared third spaces — mixed sports leagues, arts programmes and community projects — to generate organic positive interactions.
Above all, political leaders must stop exploiting religious and racial divisions for gain. Rhetoric that validates children’s prejudices undermines the very unity they are supposed to defend.

The refusal by six-year-olds to share a desk is small in scale but carries enormous weight. It is a snapshot of Malaysia at a crossroads. If treated as a minor issue, the country risks losing its social cohesion entirely.
If addressed with serious, structural reforms in education, digital literacy and political leadership, genuine unity may be possible.

In a multiethnic society, separation is not merely a social preference — it is a national security threat. Malaysia cannot afford to let its youngest generation grow up believing that difference is a threat rather than a shared reality. The time for action is now.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
85a2d653e55bd17f: Perhatikan titah Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan semasa menegur keras Menteri Besar Ismail Lasim, Jumaat lalu: "Selagi dia tak tarik apa yang dia kata tu, jangan jumpa saya, Go away, don’t see me, I don't want to see you okay? You understand?"
Dalam video yang menunjukkan Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir memarahi Ismail, si menteri besar mengangkat sembah. Adakah ini menunjukkan beliau faham lantas akur?
Apa yang mesti dilakukan Ismail atau apa yang Tuanku Muhriz mahu Ismail lakukan memang jelas jika mahu berjumpa baginda.

Tuanku Muhriz merujuk surat yang ditulis Ismail: "Ismail Lasim telah menulis surat kepada Penyimpan Mohor Besar baru-baru ini mengatakan keputusan yang dibuat bersama exco itu sah dan saya ini bukan lagi Yamtuan Negeri Sembilan."
Pada hemat saya, 'tarik balik' yang dituntut Tuanku Muhriz membawa erti Ismail mengakui atau membuat perakuan bahawa baginda masih Yang Dipertuan Besar yang sah, sekali gus menyatakan kesetiaan.
Syarat 'tarik balik' (jika ia boleh dianggap syarat) menurut saya ialah bagai satu window dalam kemelut Negeri Sembilan. Sebenarnya, sebelum ini, Yang Dipertuan Besar ada juga buka satu peluang.

Ini semasa baginda membatalkan pelantikan 10 ahli Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri atau exco pada 20 Sept lalu. Waktu itu Tuanku Muhriz meminta Ismail mempersembahkan senarai exco baharu untuk menggantikan golongan yang dipecat. Ini bagi saya satu window of opportunity for an amicable solution to the crisis.
Tidak ada senarai baharu yang dipersembahkan malah Ismail mempertikaikan pemecatan barisan exco sambil menyifatkan apa yang dilakukan tidak sah.
Ismail terlepas atau melepaskan peluang, hence we are seeing what we are seeing till today. Kemelut berpanjangan.

Mungkin Ismail ditekan Umno. Mungkin beliau rasa bertanggungjawab untuk mempertahankan barisan exco. Mungkin dia tersepit antara parti dan istana. Wallahu a'lam. Realitinya apa yang dilakukan Ismail, atau lebih tepat yang tidak dilakukan Ismail, merumitkan kemelut sehingga sekarang.

Tidak perlu saya huraikan mengapa 10 exco Ismail dipecat kerana ramai sudah maklum. Tidak perlu juga huraikan mengapa Yang Dipertuan Besar murka terhadap Ismail. Ini juga ramai sudah maklum. Yang ingin saya tegaskan ialah realitinya, Ismail sekarang keseorangan. Beliau seorang menteri besar tanpa barisan exco, boleh dikatakan menteri besar tanpa 'kerajaan'. Umno seakan mengabainya dan membiarkan beliau menghadapi krisis ini bersendirian.

Beliau dimarahi Yang Dipertuan Besar secara terbuka di hadapan khalayak. Baginda tidak mahu berjumpanya (melainkan turuti syarat). Krisis bertambah parah. Bagaimana negeri mahu ditadbir jika Yang Dipertuan Besar tidak mahu jumpa menteri besar? Bagaimana mahu menjalankan pentadbiran jika menteri besar tidak senada dengan Yang Dipertuan Besar?
Kita tahu banyak urusan pentadbiran memerlukan persetujuan raja dan menteri besar, apatah lagi si menteri besar tidak ada barisan exco.
Ismail melepaskan satu window yang dibuka Yang Dipertuan Besar dengan tidak mempersembahkan barisan exco baharu. Bagaimana pula dengan window kedua, masih berfikir-fikir atau akan dilepaskan jua?
Imbau kembali apa yang berlaku di Masjid Kampung Beting Juasseh, Kuala Pilah, Jumaat lalu. Semasa berangkat tiba Yang Dipertuan Besar sudah beri cold shoulder kepada menteri besar.
Selesai sembahyang Jumaat sebelum berangkat pulang, Yang Dipertuan Besar memarahi Ismail.
Melihat apa yang terjadi apa pilihan yang ada buat menteri besar? Saya bertanya beberapa pemerhati dan penganalisis politik, juga beberapa kawan. Jawapan mereka sama, ertinya sependapat.

9fd1af01b713f727: From Moaz Nair

In the noble effort to elevate Bahasa Melayu as the core of national identity, a topic frequently discussed among language enthusiasts is the level of mastery and fluency of the national language among multi-ethnic communities.
Most narratives typically focus on daily communication, the corporate sector, or administrative affairs.

However, from a sociolinguistic perspective, there is a dimension that is rarely explored deeply but carries significant influence over language assimilation: the use of the national language within the religious and cultural expressions of non-Muslim communities.
On one hand, there are high expectations for all citizens to anchor their lives around Bahasa Melayu. On the other, when touching upon the spiritual realm, a more complex dynamic emerges.

Understanding these contrasting approaches is not meant to assign blame, but rather to examine how language can function more inclusively as a bridge for unity without disrupting established socio-religious sensitivities.
Historical framework and the unique situation in the peninsula

The difficulty of expanding the use of Bahasa Melayu in non-Muslim religious affairs in Peninsular Malaysia is rooted in a combination of legal history, demographics, and the evolution of the language's corpus itself.

Under Article 160 of the Federal Constitution, Malay identity is clearly defined by three main elements: professing the religion of Islam, habitually speaking the Malay language, and conforming to Malay custom. This close alignment has caused Bahasa Melayu to evolve with a heavy Islamic imprint over hundreds of years through the absorption of Arabic theological terms into everyday vocabulary.

To preserve harmony and prevent theological confusion, most states in the peninsula enforce the Enactment on the Control and Restriction of the Propagation of Non-Islamic Religions, guided by the principles of Article 11(4) of the Federal Constitution. These laws restrict the use of certain religious terms to ensure the doctrinal integrity of the majority community remains protected.
Aware of these legal and social sensitivities, non-Muslim communities in the Peninsula—comprising largely Chinese and Indian ethnic groups—opt for a cautious approach.

To maintain racial harmony and safeguard their respective theological purity, they feel more comfortable retaining their mother tongues (such as Mandarin or Tamil) or English in their religious affairs. This situation inadvertently creates a linguistic divide in spiritual matters, even though they are fluent in Bahasa Melayu in other daily affairs.
Diverse models in East Malaysia and Indonesia

The reality in the peninsula presents a stark contrast when looking at the socio-political models in Sabah, Sarawak, and Indonesia. In East Malaysia, a unique demographic structure has long positioned Bahasa Melayu as the primary unifying vessel.

For hundreds of indigenous sub-ethnicities such as the Iban, Kadazandusun and Bidayuh, Bahasa Melayu has served as the daily lingua franca, including in church services and their Alkitab (Bible) texts.

The general practice and sharing of religious terms rooted in the same language are accepted with high tolerance as a historical norm, in line with the socio-political guarantees under the Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63).

Looking at our neighbour, Indonesia underwent a comprehensive language assimilation process because Bahasa Indonesia was established as a neutral and inclusive national asset. There, all recognised religions fully utilise Bahasa Indonesia in rituals and scripture translations.
Major Islamic figures and organisations like Nahdlatul Ulama (NU) and Muhammadiyah play a mature role in guiding society.
They have successfully educated the public by decoupling the language’s function as a national communication tool from the essence of an individual's personal faith.
This approach allows for the harmonious sharing of certain religious vocabularies, anchored by the concept of inter-citizen brotherhood or “ukhuwah wathaniyah”.
Building harmony through mutual understanding
These differing linguistic approaches have a tangible impact on daily social relations. In the peninsula, the separation of language in religious affairs shapes a model of "cautious coexistence".

Multi-ethnic communities deeply respect each other’s boundaries, yet opportunities for deeper cross-cultural dialogue can sometimes be limited by fears of stepping on legal sensitivities. Social interactions remain largely concentrated in secular spaces like economics, education and sports.

Conversely, the dynamics in Sabah, Sarawak and Indonesia demonstrate that when a national language is shared in the most deeply personal aspect of life—spirituality—it can erode suspicion and strengthen a sense of togetherness. The national language is no longer seen as the exclusive property of one group, but as a grand canopy sheltering all citizens.
Conclusion
The desire to see Bahasa Melayu fully embraced by all Malaysians is a noble dream that deserves support. However, discourses on elevating the language must look beyond casual conversation.

We must acknowledge the sociolinguistic challenge that arises when the national language is restricted in non-Muslim spiritual realms to safeguard faith, while simultaneously expecting these communities to assimilate the language into every facet of their lives.

To move forward, the best path is to construct a harmonious, localised understanding. Drawing from the spirit of tolerance in East Malaysia, we can begin to view Bahasa Melayu not as a tool of division, but as a bridge that unites.

Without compromising the legal protections that safeguard the faith of Muslims in the peninsula, the cultivation of the national language in cultural and literary spaces across all communities must continue to be nurtured maturely—for the future of a truly integrated Bangsa Malaysia.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

c46893703f4038fb: There is something curious about the Football Association of Malaysia (FAM) being shortlisted for the Asian Football Confederation’s (AFC) Member Association of the Year (Gold) award.

Malaysian football has spent months grappling with questions about governance, eligibility and accountability. Now its governing body is in the running for one of the region’s top administrative honours.
The winner will be announced at the AFC’s awards ceremony in Bangkok on Nov 19. FAM shares the shortlist with the FA of Hong Kong, China Limited, and the All India Football Federation.
Perhaps FAM has done enough in certain areas to merit consideration. But what exactly does the AFC reward when it names a member association of the year?
A trophy can recognise activity. It should not substitute for scrutiny of the institution behind it.

AFC general secretary Windsor John says associations submit reports on their activities and programmes. A selection panel awards points for areas such as grassroots development, youth competitions and hosting, with three associations shortlisted in each category.
Asked how the assessment treats governance and accountability, and whether strong programme delivery can offset institutional weaknesses, Windsor said:
“The assessment takes into account a wide range of areas of football in an association. You score high in some, medium in some and probably no score in other areas.”

His answer suggests that the panel assesses associations across several areas, with varying scores. But it does not explain how much weight governance carries, or whether strong results in some categories can compensate for serious weaknesses in others.
That is a fair question about an award meant to recognise an association as a whole. It does not mean the AFC ignored governance when assessing FAM.
The criteria and their weightings should make clear how institutional accountability is judged.
For FAM, the timing makes that scrutiny unavoidable.

The naturalisation scandal has damaged confidence in Malaysian football. Fifa’s sanctions over the eligibility case exposed serious failures that the national association could not brush aside with promises to move on.
The affair raised questions not only about player eligibility, but also about the controls and oversight expected of the body responsible for the national game.

September’s extraordinary congress brought another test. The Football Association of Selangor (FAS) had objected to the eligibility of the electoral committee chairman, a concern also raised by Windsor.

FAM’s electoral code, endorsed at its June 4 congress, states that the chairperson and deputy chairperson of the electoral committee must be qualified to practise law. Yet the congress proceeded amid questions over whether the committee met that requirement.
Electoral rules protect the legitimacy of the process and the people it puts in office. An association that revises its rules must follow them, even when compliance creates an inconvenient problem.
FAM cannot demand respect for its authority while treating its own rules as obstacles to negotiate away.
Governance as part of the scorecard
There is also the AFC’s audit of FAM, which many have urged the association to release in full.

Only part of the report had been presented at the extraordinary congress in June and critics argued that the public deserved to know the full findings, warning that withholding them could fuel speculation.
Prepared by AFC deputy secretary-general Vahid Kardany, the report highlighted weaknesses in governance, accountability and organisational management.
It found that FAM’s administrative structure had not received formal executive committee approval.
It also pointed to decision-making concentrated around certain individuals and critical functions heavily dependent on them.
Weak systems for retaining institutional knowledge threatened continuity and could discourage staff from raising concerns.
These are not cosmetic flaws. A sports association needs clear lines of responsibility, systems that survive leadership changes and an environment where staff can report problems without fear.
Otherwise, the institution risks becoming dependent on a handful of people rather than sound processes.
Football development raises another pressing question.

Malaysia’s U-23, U-19 and U-16 teams have struggled to remain competitive in Asean and reach the Asian stage. Their results demand scrutiny of the system meant to prepare young Malaysians for international football.
The National Football Development Programme (NFDP) was designed to produce a technically superior generation by 2025.
Yet questions persist about its outcomes, coaching standards, talent identification and the number of players progressing to senior international football.
Malaysia has repeatedly reworked its structures while regional rivals continue to develop their talent pools. Academies, coaches and thousands of trainees are not proof of success by themselves.
How many players become professionals? How many earn senior international caps? How many fulfil the promise that justified the investment?
FAM has taken on a greater role in NFDP’s technical implementation. It now has an opportunity to show what a more focused system can deliver.
Another revamp, however, is not an achievement in itself. Results must follow.
The Malaysian Football League’s problems add to the wider unease. Salary arrears and Fifa sanctions involving clubs expose persistent weaknesses in the domestic game.

FAM and the MFL are separate bodies, so responsibility for individual cases must be established rather than casually assigned to the national association. Still, activity reports alone cannot capture the health of Malaysian football.
The AFC may have sound reasons for shortlisting FAM. The nomination does not prove the panel got it wrong, nor does it mean FAM has achieved nothing worthy of recognition.

But an award bearing the title Member Association of the Year suggests more than a tally of activities. If the AFC wants the honour to command respect, it should explain how its criteria assess both an association’s output and the way it governs itself.
FAM, too, should welcome scrutiny rather than hide behind the nomination. Recognition will mean little while questions about its elections, audit findings and development record remain unanswered.
A trophy can decorate a cabinet, but it cannot repair a governing system, develop a generation of footballers or restore public confidence.
Before anyone celebrates the award, the more important question is whether the association has done the work to earn the trust that the honour is supposed to represent.

1fb61941d5b43ee1: From Jason Chuah
Malaysia has staked a good deal of its economic future on a few dozen strands of fibre lying on the seabed.

More than 20 international submarine cables land at over 10 stations in this country, and with its digital economy blueprint the government aims to make Malaysia Southeast Asia’s leading destination for cable landings.
They carry almost all of our international data, including the traffic behind Johor’s data-centre boom. Yet the criminal law that protects them was written for the telegraph.

The only provision aimed squarely at cable damage is Section 431A of the Penal Code. It punishes mischief by cutting or injuring “any electric telegraph cable, wire, line, post, instrument or apparatus for signalling”, with up to two years imprisonment or a fine.
The provision has three serious weaknesses.
First, it requires mischief, meaning intention or knowledge that loss or damage is likely.
A ship that drags its anchor across a cable through carelessness might well fall outside it, and so does one that merely claims carelessness.
That is exactly the explanation offered in almost every recent incident, from the Baltic Sea to the Taiwan Strait. Proving mischief will not be easy.
Second, it stops at the territorial sea. The Penal Code applies to offences committed “within Malaysia”, which takes in our 12-nautical-mile territorial waters but no more.
Its extraterritorial provisions reach Malaysian citizens and Malaysian-registered ships, but not a foreign crew aboard a foreign vessel.
Most of a cable’s route lies further out, in the exclusive economic zone and on the continental shelf.
The Exclusive Economic Zone Act 1984 and the Continental Shelf Act 1966 regulate the laying of cables but do not make damaging them an offence.
A foreign ship that cuts a cable 30 miles off our coast commits, so far as Malaysian criminal law is concerned, no offence at all.

Third, the language is out of date. Modern fibre-optic cables probably count as “apparatus for signalling”. The planned subsea power link carrying a gigawatt of Sarawak’s electricity to Singapore almost certainly does not.

International law regrettably does not fill the gap. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which Malaysia ratified in 1996, is better at protecting the freedom to lay cables than the cables themselves.

Article 113 obliges states to criminalise the wilful or culpably negligent breaking of cables, but only by ships flying their own flags and their own nationals. Malaysia’s law, which ignores negligence, arguably does not meet that obligation.
Worse, Article 97 says that when an “incident of navigation” occurs beyond the territorial sea, only the flag state may prosecute the master or crew.

Nor does it give any right to board a ship suspected of damaging a cable. So when a vessel flying a flag of convenience drags its anchor through a cable in our EEZ, UNCLOS refers us to a flag state that has neither the means nor the will to act.

This is not hypothetical. In May, the director-general of the Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency acknowledged that tankers carrying Iranian-linked oil choose to transfer cargo about 70km off Johor precisely to “exploit jurisdictional gaps”.
One monitoring group counted 42 such transfers there in about 10 weeks. They operate in the very waters where Malaysia’s criminal law stops.
The United Kingdom faced the same problem and offers a useful model. Its principal offence dates from 1885 but was long ago extended to the continental shelf.
In May 2026 the British government went further, announcing a new criminal framework covering damage that is intentional or reckless, with tougher penalties.
Malaysia should do three things.
First, replace section 431A with a dedicated offence covering intentional, reckless and culpably negligent damage to telecommunications and power cables, with penalties that reflect what is at stake.
Second, extend that offence expressly to the EEZ and continental shelf, applying to any person, whatever their nationality or flag.
Third, draft it with the enforcement problem in mind.
In August 2026 the Helsinki Court of Appeal revived the prosecution of the crew of the Eagle S, a shadow-fleet tanker accused of cutting cables in the Gulf of Finland.

The court held that the offence was committed where its effects were felt, in Finland. It also held that deliberate anchor-dragging is not a mere “incident of navigation” that UNCLOS reserves to the flag state.

The coastal state suffering the cable damage can therefore have criminal jurisdiction. A Malaysian statute that locates the offence where the damage is suffered, and defines it accordingly, would put our courts on the same footing.
Malaysia, which has long taken a robust view of coastal-state rights, is better placed than the great maritime powers to take this step. What it lacks is a law fit for the age of fibre.
Jason Chuah is chairman of the Board of Research at the Maritime Institute of Malaysia and an FMT reader.

32750e74423d48e7: Today, I’m talking with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media, and telecom, about SpaceX’s recently announced plan to become a major wireless carrier.

Last week, SpaceX agreed to buy a big chunk of low-band spectrum to expand the Starlink network, spectrum that’s been traded around the telecom business for decades now. SpaceX’s ambitious plan is to use that spectrum to help build “the world’s most advanced mobile network.”
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Combined with news that the FCC approved the deployment of 15,000 next-gen Starlink satellites and the company’s previous agreement to purchase close to $20 billion worth of EchoStar spectrum last year, it’s now clear SpaceX is serious about competing with AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile.

I’ve covered the telecom business for a long time, and I’ve always known that these companies can say they want to do something until they run into the harsh reality of how expensive it is to actually do it. The telecom graveyard of pivots, bad ideas, and failed acquisitions is vast.

Walt has been closely monitoring SpaceX’s acquisition, and he’s correctly predicted that the company was headed in this direction for months now. So I wanted to dig into whether SpaceX can pull this off, why Walt thinks the existing telecom giants have really fumbled their response to SpaceX’s growing threat, and what happens when Elon Musk’s rocket company jumps headfirst into a business everyone loves to hate.
Okay: LightShed Partners’ Walter Piecyk on SpaceX’s plan to expand into mobile. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Walter Piecyk, you’re a partner and a tech, media, and telecom analyst at LightShed Partners. Welcome to Decoder.
Thanks for having me. I’m looking forward to it.

I’m excited to talk to you. I feel like we’ve been tweeting or posting around each other for many, many years, but I’m a telecom nerd at heart. I’ve been covering the space for ages. SpaceX is going to make a big splash. It’s going to be the fourth major mobile carrier in the United States and maybe the world. It bought some spectrum to do it.

It’s EchoStar spectrum by way of private equity. It is at once very simple and also very complicated. Give us the state of the state. SpaceX bought 800 Mhz spectrum for $8 billion. They spent nearly $20 billion already on separate EchoStar spectrum. What is SpaceX trying to do here?

It’s definitely complicated, but maybe less complicated than trying to figure out how to put a data center out in space and making that work. Or something on the moon. But they don’t typically want to own spectrum and spend for spectrum. If you think about how Starlink was built, satellite companies don’t typically pay for spectrum. And then as the business evolved and as they saw the opportunity in telecom, they purchased some spectrum initially from EchoStar.

The feedback they got from investors at that time was very positive and they said, “Wait a minute, you should do more here.” This is a trillion-dollar enterprise value business in the US alone. Obviously they have global aspirations both for Starlink as well as what they’re doing with this mobile telephone service. So they bought more. They went back to EchoStar. That’s a key thing to pay attention to, in that they bought some spectrum and then they went back and bought some more.

Because with a lot of things that Elon Musk does, he learns as he goes. He bought the spectrum, got feedback, talked to people in telecom, and bought some more spectrum. Then we didn’t hear from them for a while. Now, you have this thing that happened last week where they bought some more spectrum, and I can go through the history of it if you care, but it’s long, wonky telecom stuff. This was originally the Nextel spectrum, if you remember that company.

I do. Actually, I do want you to go through the history because I think the telecom business is best understood as a bunch of lobbyists trying to make everything more complicated than it should be. Yes, spectrum auctions are complicated and what spectrum is good for what is deeply tied to the physics of the radio spectrum and all that.

But here it’s the 800 MHz spectrum from the Nextel service, the old push-to-talk, walkie-talkie service that Sprint had to divest as part of the deal to get sold to T-Mobile. They’ve been trying to sell it for ages. They sold it to this company, Grain Management. They’ve been sitting on it, and when Starlink showed up, Elon bought it. Nobody else wanted it. What did he see in the spectrum that no one else did?

When you realize that you need to build a terrestrial network to support what you’re doing with satellites, because satellites work fine if you’ve got your dish on the top of your house and you’re getting your broadband, but when you’re trying to connect with a phone that doesn’t have the same type of power or you’re going inside a home, you’re going to need better coverage.

Sirius Satellite also has supplementary towers. There are not that many of them, but sometimes when you get out of Sirius coverage, you will connect to a tower. When they bought that EchoStar spectrum and then got FCC approval, and if you looked into those details of that FCC approval and what was required, you would see that they can’t do this by satellites alone. There had to be terrestrial.

Then SpaceX, as Elon is wont to do, tries to send some diversions like, “We’re going to do Femtocell, we’re not going to do macrocell, this, that, and the other thing.” But they realized that they were going to build a terrestrial network. Now they finally realized, “If I’m going to offer mobile service, I need some form of a terrestrial network.”

At the same time, the telcos are not going to help them out. They’re not going to give them a wholesale agreement. Then when they go back and say the companies that had the lowest churn, what is the fundamental value you need in a terrestrial network? It’s low-band spectrum. Why? It travels further, you can get better coverage, and you have that connectivity.

So getting this low-band spectrum piece was just an important part, not to make the satellites work better, but to actually give them the spectrum assets that they need to build a terrestrial network. That’s why the stocks reacted, because people finally came to terms with the fact that Elon is actually going to build a terrestrial network.

I’m less interested in the stock and more interested in just the cost structure of how this works. If I rewind my brain to being a baby blogger at Engadget 100 years ago, the FCC told all the TV networks they had to stop broadcasting on 700 MHz and we were going to run an auction.

Verizon and AT&T bought big chunks of 700 MHz spectrum and that’s what 4G is built on. That’s the low-bandwidth spectrum that you’re talking about. It goes everywhere. This was a big victory that we reallocated 700 MHz, and 800 MHz was sitting right there the whole time. This is the Nextel spectrum. If it is so valuable, why wasn’t there a market for it until Elon showed up just now?

It was part of this transaction. T-Mobile ended up having to sell it because the government said, “If we’re going to allow you to take out the fourth competitor, which was Sprint, then in order to enable another fourth competitor out there, we need to have you guys give up some of your low-band spectrum.”

Part of the deal that T-Mobile and Sprint had with the government was that they would sell it to EchoStar. Why? Because Charlie Ergen, CEO of Dish at the time — it’s EchoStar now — was going to be the fourth competitor. This was the rationale that they gave in terms of the approval of the transaction. Dish needed low-band spectrum. The problem is Ergen went about his business, he was trying to build a network, and then he just couldn’t afford to buy that.

They had the rights to buy. Then at that point when Ergen failed on the bid to come up with the dollars to buy that spectrum, it enabled T-Mobile and actually forced them to put it up for auction. Now, your question: Why didn’t someone else show up then? Again, from SpaceX’s standpoint, as I mentioned at the start of this podcast, their strategy has been evolving over time.

In terms of the other telcos, they can’t really use it. There are some limitations that they have. But in hindsight, maybe Verizon or AT&T should have bought this 800 MHz spectrum for whatever it was, let’s call it $8 billion. They’re probably losing more in enterprise value over the concerns of what’s happening with SpaceX than what it cost them just to buy it in what’s known as foreclose. They basically just take it, even if they don’t use it or do whatever they need to meet those build out requirements and stop SpaceX from having unnecessary assets. I don’t think even these companies were taking Elon seriously and thinking that he would actually build the network.

Do you think that’s colored by the failure of Dish? We covered the promises of Dish Network to build a fourth wireless carrier in this country so closely. Their attempt was predicated on some amount of technology innovation.

They were going to build this thing called an O-RAN network, which had a more competitive supplier base instead of just Nokia or Siemens or whoever, and they were going to run it on AWS and that was going to reduce costs. Man, eventually they supported one Motorola handset in Vegas and even that was backstopped by AT&T. They literally could not do it. These promises never came true. Dish is a different company and Charlie Ergen’s a different CEO and their ability to just throw money at a problem until it’s solved is very different from Elon.

But if they couldn’t innovate to make a cheaper, faster network, what’s the evidence that Starlink can stand up an entire terrestrial network at a cost basis that allows them to compete selling service to consumers, while they’re also standing up an entire network in space? Because that feels like adding up a lot of cost.

I’m going to go back even deeper than that. Remember when Sprint was struggling, Masayoshi Son from SoftBank was claiming the same thing. They were going to cut their CapEx to nothing and they were going to use these small cells. They innovated how wireless was going to get delivered. That failed. Obviously, they had to get bailed out through the purchase when T-Mobile bought Sprint effectively for just the spectrum.

That network got completely decommissioned. To your point, Dish got a network built, but they couldn’t resonate in the market. The difference between Dish and SpaceX is Elon’s ability to get customers. That’s where Dish truly failed. They built the network. The network worked fine. They had the wholesale agreements that they needed.

I’ll push back on you a little bit there. I have a very funny email from a Dish PR person from several years ago where they said, “We’d like to issue a correction to your story. Our network does exist.” That was the level that they were competing at, where they had to insist to us that the network was real, even though we could not find it in our tests in the various cities they claim.
Maybe there was a network, they built some amount of network, but they had not built anything that competed at the national scale with the big three.

Absolutely. It’s not like your phone. The phone that I was using, I had an iPhone that it was mostly going to roam onto the AT&T and T-Mobile wholesale agreements that existed. The theory is you get the customers, you have a go-to-market strategy, and then you backfill the network. This is probably going to be something similar.

You can even go back to when John Legere first took over T-Mobile. They had a crappy network, and then Legere promised, “We’re going to build it,” taking on customers saying that the network was great before the network was great. Then it caught up because they actually finally got the Germans, Deutsche Telekom, to give them the money to invest in the network.

The same thing can happen here where SpaceX will sell something that’ll probably rely on other assets that are out there, even if the telcos themselves are circling the wagons. They have the satellites for certain benefits in terms of coverage and then they can build the capacity over time. The point is it’s going to take time. You can’t just turn on a network overnight and start selling service on that.

This has always been my framework of how to think about telecom companies. You can try to run the network cheaper or you can run some kind of different technology to make that cheaper. Or you can just spend and have the best network, which was the Verizon strategy for years and years and years.

Then you’ve got to acquire and manage your customers. That was the T-Mobile strategy. That was John Legere. He was just nicer to people than AT&T was, and he picked up a lot of customers and that drove some investment.

Then you’ve got to get some devices. You have to have the iPhone. We can set that aside because it feels like that era of competition is over. We’re not doing exclusive devices anymore. But those are the two. I’m just looking at the network here. It does not seem to me, from the outside, that Starlink is proposing to build a cheaper network.

It feels like they’re proposing to build a vastly more expensive network because they need the satellites. They’re going to launch 15,000 more satellites to support this network. Then they’re going to build a terrestrial network by investing in spectrum on the ground and building some set of base stations.

Then they’re going to have to convince one of the big three to let them roam over as some sort of mobile virtual network operator (MVNO). The big three do not want to do that. So they’re going to overcharge them for that. I’m just stuck at that being a lot of cost, even if you’re Elon Musk and you can make some set of people buy whatever you’re selling.

The third thing you said is obviously the most challenging. That’s the tent and the pole that prevents you from launching services sooner rather than later. But without necessarily getting a wholesale agreement, there might be other ways. Roaming agreements exist out there. There are roaming partners that exist that these telcos still rely on. It’s very expensive. It’s not something you can build a high-margin business on, but it perhaps provides an entry to the market sooner rather than later.

As Apple has pitched in terms of satellite connectivity, some people are in the middle of the Utah desert texting because they’re injured. There’s value there. But it’s the soccer field. We have, maybe not in the cities, but in the suburbs, plenty of areas that the telcos have effectively given up on trying to provide coverage because of NIMBY-ism, meaning people just don’t want these cell sites. This satellite coverage can give you not just this basic text messaging that Apple has been doing through the Globalstar constellation, but a true cellphone-type experience.

So that’s a positive. The second differentiation is the fact that these telcos have 60 percent earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) margins. So there’s a lot of fat there that can be eaten off of, that when you’re selling other services in terms of Elon, like home broadband, maybe this becomes an entree in terms of pushing Grok and people’s usage. You don’t necessarily need 60 percent margins, in this case, for him to justify building this network.

They also talk about other data connectivity that these satellites are going to enable. Again, in the current constellation, you need a lot of power and you need a dish. But if you don’t have that, if you have the cell phone-type power, then the internet of things (IOT) and other types of opportunities that exist there become another revenue opportunity that they look at.

It’s just funny. The IOT story — that’s what all these companies promised us about 4G. That’s what they all promised us about 5G. There’s something about this business that just rhymes every time. They’re going to do self-driving cars and robot surgery. I’m confident we’re going to hear about self-driving cars and robot surgery when it comes to Starlink and Tesla and Optimus.

There’s something about these applications for next generation networks that just recurs, and we hear about them all the time. Then I think about our consumer audience at The Verge, and they want long battery life and fast service and [connectivity] all the places they go. I’m not sure how that squares with your phone is going to connect directly to a satellite in the middle of a soccer field. There’s something about that that also seems challenging.

It’s just the performance if your phone does connect to the satellite on the soccer field and it works. A lot of the things that people said wouldn’t work on Starlink in terms of airplanes or even getting customer-premises equipment (CPE) down below a certain price, they’ve delivered on. Obviously, Elon sometimes delivers on them a little later than some of his initial optimistic promises, but they ultimately get delivered on.

There is the ability with these new constellations to give you that type of connectivity on these spaces. Is that enough to differentiate with consumers? I don’t know. The telcos have attacked this by saying, “No one cares about our direct-to-device (D2D) services.” Well, your D2D services are not good. It’s just sending basic text messages. What they’re talking about is giving you that blanket coverage where you get what you expect from your cell phone wherever you go.

That’s fine, but you still have to give it to the person in the middle of the building where their cell phone works today and provide the volume at a cost that is going to be attractive to that consumer. So those are longer-term things that are going to require some amount of terrestrial network build. Then the question is: how much? A lot of the attacks that have been out there have been referencing $100 billion, $200 billion. I get that. Why?

Telcos each spend $10 billion to $15 billion a year, but they are maintaining massive customer bases. To get that initial network up where you have that usage, where you use that low-band spectrum to get into buildings, is not those types of numbers. You’re probably talking like $10 billion, $15 billion for that initial build in terms of CapEx.

The dynamic there is really interesting. I’m just thinking about AT&T when the iPhone came out. The network immediately got overloaded because there was a surge of customer demand that took four years to truly resolve. Part of that resolution was just putting the iPhone on the other carriers.

How do you think that will play out for Starlink here? Because right now, Starlink customer service is not the best in the industry. Their actual service, people love it. And then when they need customer service, it’s a bunch of automated systems and people complaining on Reddit. So there’s some challenge there if you’re running a consumer business at this scale.

For consumer businesses, think about all the advertising that’s done. The fulfillment, dealing with the phones, phone subsidies, and that’s a big part of the financing. How many customers are we talking about? So for the amount of spectrum that they have now in the network that I’m talking about for $10–$15 billion, you’re not taking 50 percent share overnight. I don’t think that would be that expectation from day one.

44e84b9497a21540: Late Sunday night, a still-unknown cybercriminal or group hacked thousands of remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of French grocery stores, spiking temperatures, spoiling food, and sparking fires. This is part of an ongoing trend of attacking physical systems that can do damage in the real world. In August, a ransomware attack disrupted building-management systems at a Canadian hospital, affecting door access controls, central HVAC monitoring, and the issuing of staff access cards. And three years ago, cyberattacks hit Las Vegas casinos, causing slot machines to go dark, preventing payment kiosks and ATMs from spitting out cash, and locking guests out of their rooms when the electronic keys stopped working. Not all digital intrusions remain in cyberspace, and attackers don’t need to encrypt files and steal data to cause chaos. Hitting physical systems often produces more severe consequences - and turns up the heat on executives to pay an extortion demand. “There was one gig where the customer was refusing to pay, and so the threat actor was like, ‘Hold my beer, have fun getting into your offices,’ and locked everybody out,” Tim Beasley, a senior incident response consultant at Semperis, told The Register. Beasley won’t name the customer, or provide any incriminating information, but said the incident response involved police smashing glass in addition to his team recovering compromised data. “The cops had to break in, and literally get into the building, breaking some windows, so the customer was able to finally get back in,” he said. We asked if the customer paid the ransom demand, and Beasley yelled: “Oh, hell, no!” A report published earlier this month by ServiceNow’s Armis Labs found increasing evidence of ransomware attackers using physical consequences as leverage in their intrusions. “Today’s BAS operate at the intersection of IT and OT worlds, creating unprecedented exposure,” the report said. Ransomware with physical consequences Building automation systems - BAS - are the critical systems that control and monitor facilities’ HVAC, lighting, energy usage, and water consumption. They also oversee badge readers, door locks, surveillance cameras, fire alarm control panels, and other physical safety equipment. As such, BAS make very attractive targets for ransomware operators looking for high-pressure ways to extort organizations into paying multi-million ransom demands. These systems also appeal to government-backed goons and hacktivists looking to ensure maximum psychological and physical impact during destructive cyberattacks. Armis Labs found 73 percent of organizations own BAS that have been used in ransomware attacks, and this same percentage have known exploited vulnerabilities in at least one of their building automation systems. Additionally, 91 percent of BAS communicate over insecure protocols - opening up an even bigger attack surface for cyber-miscreants wanting to cause physical harm. “The primary thing that we see with any attack on building management systems or physical systems: It’s a great place for the threat actor to hide,” Michael Freeman, ServiceNow’s senior director of threat research, told The Register. “It's easier for them to compromise, and it's easier for them to hide in.” BAS and operational technology (OT) in general have fewer security controls than IT systems. Most require continual uptime, which makes them harder to patch or even scan for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations as this may lead to outages. “One case in particular, against a very large financial institution, the threat actors were staying low and quiet by attacking their BMS systems, and then pivoting into the IT environment,” Freeman said. The intruders were routinely caught - and booted from - the financial institution’s IT systems, so they built backdoors into the BMS to ensure persistent access to both OT and IT networks. “We're also seeing threat actors using AI to understand more building automation systems, especially ones that are using obscure OSs like VxWorks, older Unix-type systems,” Freeman said. AI has entered the chat As multiple security experts have told us in previous interviews, security through obscurity is dead. Not only does AI make it easier for attackers to find bugs – some very obscure and decades old - but it also means criminals no longer need to be OT experts to carry out destructive cyberattacks on critical networks and facilities. Instead, they can use AI to learn all about the obscure protocols and proprietary hardware and software that historically made industrial control systems black boxes. “It’s easier to understand what the controls are,” Freeman said, using the example of an attacker trying to take down a plane, or some similar catastrophic cyberattack. Historically, even advanced, government-backed hacking squads would “be quiet, because you don't know what changing certain settings is going to do,” Freeman explained. “Now you can use AI to say, ‘If I compromise a weight and balance system for airlines, all I need to do now is move this number here to this number, and I just told the system to load heavy stuff on the right side of the plane instead of equal distribution.'” Freeman told us he has seen attackers break into airlines’ OT gear in the past. “But they didn’t know what they were getting into, and so they left them alone,” he said. “Those do cause me concern because in the past I've helped to kick people out of those types of systems.” Industrial orgs increasingly under attack OT security provider Dragos tracks ransomware groups’ claims against industrial organizations on the criminals’ leak sites, along with publicly disclosed intrusions affecting manufacturing and other critical sectors. To be clear: claims on leak sites aren’t always accurate or even true, and the claim itself doesn’t mean operations or control systems were hit. Since 2022, however, “the numbers have been consistently increasing,” Lexie Mooney, senior threat analyst at Dragos, told The Register. The cybersecurity firm tracked 995 ransomware attacks against industrial orgs in 2023, a 49.5 percent increase from 2022. That number jumped more than 87 percent in 2024. Active ransomware groups targeting industrial orgs also grew in 2024 to 80 groups, up from 50 the year before. Dragos tracked 119 ransomware groups impacting more than 3,300 industrial organizations in 2025, and the incidents have steadily increased every quarter this year: 1,020 incidents in the first quarter of 2026 and 1,140 incidents in Q2. “The vast majority of cases are opportunistic,” Abdul Alamri, a senior threat analyst at Dragos, told us. “In some of the cases that we have seen an operational impact, either physical systems or an OT operation, it’s just the nature of the opportunism on the part of those ransomware groups.” This is partially due to the complexity of OT systems, he added. “Ransomware groups want to disrupt operations, and put pressure on the victims to pay the ransom,” Alamri said. “They don’t want to invest that time and effort to target complex systems." It’s usually quicker and easier for financially motivated crims to affect operations via IT systems - as the extortionists did in the August 2025 Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) breach, which halted manufacturing and crippled business operations for months. Internet-connected OT: the next 'low-hanging fruit' The other side of this complexity, however, is that many organizations themselves still lack visibility into their OT environments. Dragos estimates that fewer than 10 percent of OT networks worldwide currently have sufficient network monitoring in place. Plus, in 30 percent of incidents the security firm responded to in 2025, the investigations did not begin with a detection alert, but with someone noticing that “something seemed wrong” in operations. This lack of visibility, combined with threats from AI, worries Alamri. “If you compare the risk that we have seen from humans, to what we are about to face in the near future with AI agents who might continuously try to break into those systems - it’s a pretty dark future if we don't take the right measures to protect ourselves against it.” As organizations get better at patching and securing IT systems, attackers will likely look to internet-connected OT systems where digital compromises have real-world consequences, according to Matt Hayden, VP of cyber and emerging threats at General Dynamics Information Technology. “We all anticipate that as we get better at reducing the IT low-hanging fruit, OT will become a vector of much more scrutiny and much more attention,” Hayden told The Register. Before joining GDIT, Hayden served as the assistant secretary for cyber, infrastructure, risk and resilience policy at the US Department of Homeland Security. Compliance vs. security “There is a big focus on the hardware being connected for the purpose of compliance - and to make sure that, in the name of compliance, we aren't opening back doors, to devices that traditionally wouldn't have to be connected to facilitate their service,” he said, using refrigeration units as an example of one such system that is now internet-connected for compliance purposes. This was prior to the French supermarket hacks. Refrigeration units’ monitoring systems connect to the internet so their owners and operators can prove to regulators that the units maintain their uptime and temperature in accordance with regulations. “So if the health department comes by, they say, ‘Look, my refrigerator was at 27 degrees for the last 72 days,' and they have a check mark, and they get their A plus. But that simple connectivity is also a vector in which that particular refrigerant unit could be targeted for disruption,” Hayden said. About a week after our interview, criminals did exactly that. “The recently reported exploitations of commercial refrigeration units represent a significant example of devices without digital value, no sensitive data or extended enterprise access, being exploited by being connected to the internet with unpatched firmware,” Hayden told us in a subsequent email. He said he expects the attribution to be “less nation-state, and more likely those looking for targets of opportunity to identify what could be done with the unpatched systems.” “The consequences are food supply degradation at a small scale, but it is an important example of what could happen at scale very quickly with more consequential operating equipment,” Hayden said.®
a73522a3fefcaa29: Close to 1 billion meetings take place each day around the world. CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings. Planning for and spearheading meetings eats up the lion’s share of managers’ time. In much of the industrialized world, meetings are both the metronomes and menaces of people’s working lives.

Given the enormous time spent in workplace meetings, do we know what they accomplish or how to make them as worthwhile as possible? For decades, the answer was… not really. Meetings weren’t a particularly accessible subject of study. But that has changed. Once a tiny niche area, “meeting science” is a growing specialization among organizational and social psychologists. The field is accelerating as archived virtual meetings provide vast swaths of data. And it is providing a fascinating window into human behavior.

Meeting to talk helps fulfill basic human needs to connect, communicate, and cooperate. People have long come together—in caves, fields, market squares, and town halls—to get something done, share ideas, get on the same page, or just to remark on the weather. But meeting scientists define their subject as gatherings of people “with some goal or structure to the event,” says organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology, who coauthored a review of over three decades of meeting science in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior.

d9ad1ab514e787dd: From P Kamalanathan
Last week, a young student at AIMST University asked me: “Datuk, did Rajinikanth go to university?”
I smiled.
Rajini studied in a Kannada-medium school and worked as a coolie, carpenter and bus conductor in Bangalore.
He joined a film institute at 25, an age when we tell our youth, “You are late.”
Last week, Jailer 2 was breaking box-office records again. At 74, he is still a superstar.
We celebrate his punchlines, but we ignore his lessons on education.
As a former deputy minister of education who oversaw five million students, I see five lessons from Rajini that our new National Education Plan 2026-2035 is trying to teach.
First: Learning agility beats certificates
Rajini had no degree. But he had what the ministry now calls “learning agility”. From stage plays to learning Hindi for Andha Kanoon to learning motion capture for Enthiran, he never stopped.
In Switzerland this year, I saw Swiss CEOs with no MBAs but 10 micro-credentials in AI. That is the Rajini model: lifelong TVET.
Second: Discipline is education
Director SP Muthuraman once said that Rajini was the first to arrive and the last to leave. In 50 years, there has been no “Rajini late” headline.
We chase tuition, but our students fail because they cannot wake up at 6am. Discipline, like that of the Bangalore bus conductor punching tickets at 5am, is the first certificate.
Third: Humility is Karamah Insaniah
The National Education Plan speaks of Karamah Insaniah, or the recognition and uplifting of human dignity. Look at Rajini.
He is a superstar, yet he sits on the floor, touches elders' feet and says, “I am a small child of K Balachander.”
In an age of TikTok arrogance, he teaches adab. My mother always taught me that education without humility is noise.
Fourth: Reinvention in the AI age

Rajini, at 74, is learning AI filmmaking for Jailer 2. If a 74-year-old can act with de-ageing technology, our youth can earn Google AI certification, which the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) offers free in Selangor.
Fifth: Do well, do good

Rajini famously said, “Money comes, goes. Give.” He built schools quietly. This is what I tell my colleagues at the Public Relations Practitioners Society of Malaysia: sustainability is a competitive advantage. Rajini has sustained a 50-year career because people trust his goodness.
That student asked if Rajini passed his exams. I told him: He did not pass with straight As, but he passed the hardest exam: life.
This Deepavali, when we watch Rajini on screen, let us tell our children:
Don’t copy his style; copy his discipline.
Don’t just whistle for the superstar; learn to be a superstar in your own trade, whether as a welder, coder or teacher.
Because, as Rajini said in Padayappa: “En vazhi, thani vazhi”, or “My way is my own way”.
Let our education system allow every Malaysian child to find their own way.
