a869668709f8a0e3: From Terence Netto
Zahir Hassan, the PKR MP for Wangsa Maju, is on to something.
Although he says he is friendly with Rafizi Ramli, he is not about to leave PKR for Bersama, the new political party PKR dissidents are gravitating to.
Perhaps what Zahir is saying is that he likes Rafizi’s ideas but he is not about to abandon PKR to join Bersama.
It may be that Zahir wants to encourage individuals and parties that have sprouted up on the broad expanse of the movement for reformasi to adopt a spirit of bipartisanship.
Such a spirit will avert the fragmentation of that expanse into multiple political parties, each following the instincts of its restless initiator.
This is a recipe for ideological incoherence and wasted energy.
One would have thought the formation of Bersama would have slowed the fragmentation of the reformasi landscape into multiple parties and representatives.
This has not been the case.
Parti Bangsa Malaysia, set up by Julau MP Larry Sng, was fledging since its formation in 2021, but after Bersama’s launch earlier this year, it gained a frisson of energy.

Larry drew former DAP stalwart Ronnie Liu to energise PBM and this saw lawyer and social activist Siti Kassim signing up in the cause. She was followed into the party by Shamsul Saad, who fronts the popular Gut Shot Podcast.

Shamsul and cohort Syed Akhbar Ali are two of the most trenchant commentators on public affairs in Malaysia, the former having gone on to declare he intends to stand for election in GE16 and even wants to become prime minister.
This is what happens when the leader – Anwar Ibrahim – who had for a long time wanted to become prime minister, did not become the prime minister they wanted him to be: a host of wannabes appear.
They think it is easy to do what Anwar appears to find difficult: follow an agenda long enunciated and espoused.
Presently, we have a plethora of parties and contenders for running Putrajaya and for prime minister.
But on the broad expanse of the reformasi agenda, we have essentially Pakatan Harapan and Bersama, with PBM lately in the fray.
Not much point in talking about Muda and Parti Sosialis Malaysia.
This is not to disparage the two, but they are perennial also-rans.
As for Muhyiddin Yassin-led Bersatu, it is headed for collaboration with PKR, not only in the upcoming Melaka polls but also in GE16.
This brings us to what Zahir is intimating when he says his friendship with Rafizi is not prompting him to sign up with Bersama.
The Bersatu rump, after the breakaway of Wawasan, will find its way back to PKR.
So would Bersama.
Of course, this would be after Anwar leaves the scene.
At 79, his retirement is not too far away.
The political landscape that supports reformasi cannot sustain multiple parties.
They have all to get together, arrayed against a coalition between an Islamic PAS and a right-wing Umno, which if it comes about, is certain to be shaky.
But that matter is for another day.
A spirit of bipartisanship, as intimated by Zahir, is what will get the reformists together, a consolidation that’s necessary to avert a PAS-Umno triumph.
The reformasi crowd do not all have to agree on everything; they just have to collate essence from miscellany.
As Zahir has argued, a new spirit of bipartisanship will require maturity from the reformists.
They will have to be wary of the egoists and the self-centred and plump for the true and tested.
This maturity is imperative to keep the religious identity and racial identity politics of PAS and Umno at bay.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
f01d189e282f995b: A pointed and loaded question has been raised about a minister’s decision to resign. Apparently, he has been doing his job well — “What is wrong with him? What is wrong with his work?”
The problem is corruption, theft (sakau) and misappropriation. Yet, the focus is on the future of a beleaguered secretary-general of a political party.
The party’s defeats in recent state elections speak for themselves, reflecting both the state of affairs within the party and the calibre of its leaders, whether ministers or otherwise.
It is perceived, rightly or wrongly, that the party has not been able to make much headway on issues central to its support base, notwithstanding some peripheral achievements.
Viewed in the light of the number of parliamentary seats it holds, this is most disconcerting.
Perhaps the resignation should be viewed through these lenses to gain a more holistic perspective, rather than through the narrow lens of self-serving political interests.

Doing one’s job well is not the sole criterion for maturity. One must appreciate the three branches of government — the executive, the judiciary and the legislature (Parliament). Above these is the monarchy, given that Malaysia is not a republic.
The judiciary examines the facts and determines whether a person has broken the law. It has the power to impose custodial sentences.

The Pardons Board, chaired by the monarch, exists to grant pardons to those found guilty. It operates according to its own rules and criteria governing pardons. Whether a pardon is conditional or unconditional is not the point. That is the crux of the matter.

Some have gone out on a limb to question whether the monarch is “obliged” to follow the views of the other members of the board, or whether the ruler has absolute discretion to decide on the type of pardon to be granted.

Section 40A of the Federal Constitution has been bandied about. However, one must also take into account how the courts have ruled on matters relating to this provision when decisions have been challenged.

One must appreciate that the Pardons Board is part of the broader institutional ecosystem. One cannot clap one’s hands in glee when one part of the ecosystem functions according to one’s wishes — especially when certain individuals are found guilty — only to turn against the system and declare, “I will resign”, when another part of the same system makes an “unwelcomed” decision.
One cannot have one’s cake and eat it too. Either one accepts the system in its entirety or exits it completely and seeks another domain where all one’s desires might come true!

It appears that the role of the Pardons Board has been politicised. This should not be the case. It is a matter of public record which political party the federal territories minister, who is a member of the Pardons Board, belongs to. Is there an ulterior motive or an unspoken desire to “have it my own way”?
This is highly disturbing. A pressure group comprising retired civil servants, along with several other social groups, is seeking the minutes of the Pardons Board’s meetings.
What purpose would this serve?

Perhaps these groups should redirect their attention to the internal investigation into former Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission chief Azam Baki over the issue of shareholdings. To date, the public remains in the dark about the scope and extent of the investigation, as well as whether any breaches have been identified.
We can debate the use of the word “shall” and whether it imposes a binding obligation on the monarch to follow the advice of the other members of the Pardons Board.

To some, the debate reflects disrespect for the monarchy, whose head chairs the board. It should be noted that the Constitution contains no subclause requiring the minutes of the board’s meetings to be made public or providing for the general public to debate their contents and propose an alternative course of action.

If it did, the monarch’s role would be rendered superfluous. The institution’s role within the broader ecosystem must be respected and appreciated. Decisions should not be challenged merely on the basis of political preferences.
If any minister wishes to resign, he should do so now. A conditional pardon has already been granted.

If there is chagrin and dismay, and one is unable to appreciate the institutional framework that allows for both convictions and subsequent pardons, regardless of the reasons, then resignation should be immediate.
The country is better off without leaders whose interests are so parochial.
As for other pressure groups, they should find something more worthwhile to do, especially if they comprise retired civil servants who receive handsome pensions funded by taxpayers.
Let us not engage in political gymnastics by postponing a resignation until the day a house-arrest arrangement or other conditions come to pass. Move on and prepare for GE16.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
72fbe35fa8e3b875: From Moaz Nair

When hundreds of thousands of Malaysian students wait anxiously for their SPM results, or their peers across the causeway scan the O-Level boards, they are told that they are being evaluated purely on merit.
Educational syndicates proudly market these high-stakes gauntlets as “criterion-based” — an absolute measure of what a student knows, independent of anyone else.
But behind closed doors, a very different statistical reality plays out.

Contrary to what has been assumed to be criterion-based, Cambridge IGCSE and O-Level systems do not use fixed score thresholds. Instead of a rigid “90% equals an A*” rule, Cambridge adjusts grade boundaries after every exam series based on the difficulty of the specific test papers.

While the system evaluates students against fixed learning criteria, it incorporates statistical screening to ensure fairness; if an exam paper is exceptionally difficult, the mark required for a top grade drops.
This flexible approach ensures that a grade reflects the same level of achievement from year to year, without placing strict quotas or caps on how many students can earn an A* (A-star).

Almost all major examination boards — including our own Examination Syndicate (Lembaga Peperiksaan) and Singapore Examinations and Assessment Board (SEAB) — quietly layer norm-referenced adjustments on top of raw marks.

Colloquially known as “grading on a curve” or “standard fixing”, this hidden mathematical machinery ensures that an “A” earned in an unexpectedly brutal exam year holds the exact same currency as an “A” from an easier year.
While it keeps national systems stable, this invisible balancing act is reaching a dangerous tipping point, triggering a global reckoning over student burnout and economic reality.
How the curve secretly rules the world
Different countries mask or embrace this statistical architecture in unique ways, shaping how students progress into universities and the workforce.
Malaysia’s SPM operates on a “standard fixing” model — a criterion-related, norm-referenced hybrid.
While strict subject rubrics exist, the exact raw score thresholds required to secure an A+, A, or A- shift dynamically year-by-year based on the national cohort’s overall performance curve.
In the UK, the Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulations (Ofqual) uses a policy called “Comparable Outcomes”.

By mapping the current batch of A-Level students against how they performed years ago on their childhood exams, they mathematically predict what percentage should get top grades today, adjusting the grade boundaries to match.
Singapore, in collaboration with Cambridge Assessment, maintains a fiercely competitive system where cohort distributions fine-tune final grades.
This ensures consistent standards across different generations of test-takers competing for fixed tertiary slots.

South Korea’s Suneung, a high-stakes eight-hour college scholastic ability test, completely discards raw scores for standard percentiles. Under Suneung only the top 4% of the entire country can ever secure a Tier 1 grade.
Similarly, Australia scales different subjects against one another to output the Australian Tertiary Admission Rank — a pure percentile rank from 0.00 to 99.95.

In the US, the College Board uses a process called “equating” for the college admission test, known as “SAT”. Instead of scaling you against the people in the room on test day, they map your performance against a universal “norm group” of historical test-takers to ensure a score of 700 means the same thing today as it did a decade ago.
A fundamental trade-off
The tension between norm-referenced and criterion-referenced systems comes down to a fundamental trade-off between institutional fairness and individual well-being.

On one hand, norm-referenced grading acts as a safety net. If an exam board accidentally sets an impossibly difficult Mathematics paper, the curve automatically drops the required mark for an “A”, protecting students from being penalised for the year they happened to be born.
It also provides universities with an incredibly clean, efficient filter to select top-tier applicants.
However, the dark side is a toxic, zero-sum environment. It breeds a culture where a peer’s failure directly benefits your grade.

Worse, it masks systemic educational failures. If an entire generation’s literacy or mathematical mastery drops due to prolonged disruptions, standard-fixing can hide the rot by keeping the national percentage of A’s completely stable.
Intentional or not, using standard-fixing as a political shock absorber risks severing the link between a student’s certificate and their actual, real-world proficiency.

When the curve is adjusted to ensure pass rates remain palatable, it acts less like an objective academic yardstick and more like cosmetic anaesthesia, hiding structural damage under a layer of predictable percentages.

Ultimately, centralised exam boards face an impossible mandate: they are asked to be absolute measuring tapes of human knowledge, yet they must function as traffic cops for a finite number of university seats and corporate slots.
By choosing the stability of the curve over the raw truth of student capability, our educational systems have sacrificed individual transparency for macro convenience.

Until we reconcile this contradiction, we will continue to subject hundreds of thousands of students to a game where the rules are hidden, the goalposts move, and a peer’s failure remains the secret ingredient to one’s own success.
The bell curve may keep the system level, but it is flattening the very minds it claims to measure.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
2deb8e88fd91276a: Kita tahu tiga hari lalu Hakim Noor Ruwena Md Nurdin di Mahkamah Tinggi Kuala Lumpur menolak permohonan Najib Razak untuk tangguh hukuman penjara 15 tahun dan denda RM11.4 bilion yang dijatuhkan ke atasnya setelah didapati bersalah dalam kes 1MDB. Kita tahu Najib mesti menjalani hukuman itu sebaik tempoh hukuman bersabit kesalahan kes SRC International dilengkapi. Ringkasnya habiskan hukuman kes SRC International dahulu, kemudian jalani pula hukuman kes 1MDB.

Kita juga tahu hukuman asal untuk Najib dalam kes SRC International ialah penjara 12 tahun dan denda RM210 juta, kemudian dikurangkan kepada penjara 6 tahun dan denda RM50 juta berikutan pengampunan Yang di-Pertuan Agong ke-16 Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah pada 2024. Pada 14 Okt lalu, Yang di-Pertuan Agong Sultan Ibrahim berkenan Najib diberi pengampunan bersyarat yakni menghabiskan baki hukuman penjara bawah tahanan rumah. Namun mesti bayar denda RM50 juta terlebih dahulu. Diulangi itu bersabit kes SRC International.

Untuk konteks, permohonan Najib untuk menangguhkan pelaksanaan hukuman bersabit kes 1MDB telah ditolak mahkamah, Rabu lalu. Maknanya andai Najib bayar denda RM50 juta untuk membolehkan dia menjalani tahanan rumah, Najib tetap akan kembali ke penjara pada Ogos 2028 untuk memulakan hukuman penjara 15 tahun pula kerana hukuman kes SRC International tamat pada 23 Ogos 2028.

Tentunya ramai dalam Umno tidak suka. Umno memang mengikuti rapat kes Najib dan setiap perkembangan yang tidak memihak kepada bekas presiden mereka diterima dengan sugul dan marah. Umno tetap mempertahankan Najib meskipun pelbagai peringkat dalam sistem kehakiman negara mendapati dia bersalah. Ini membawa saya kepada artikel ini, ditulis oleh kolumnis FMT Tajuddin Rasdi bertajuk 'Teori kenapa orang Melayu terima pemimpin perasuah'.
Penulisan Tajuddin mendapat reaksi seorang ahli Pemuda Umno bernama Salahuddin Hamzah. Beliau menolak teori Tajuddin. "Saya sangat marah dengan teori itu," kata Salahuddin.

Dalam menidakkan pendapat Tajuddin, beliau berkata persepsi terhadap rasuah berada pada tahap kemuncak susulan skandal 1MDB antara 2014 hingga 2018. Apa yang berlaku selepas itu? Umno-Barisan Nasional ditolak secara besar-besaran oleh rakyat selepas memerintah negara selama 60 tahun. Pada 2022 pula BN hanya memenangi 30 kerusi.

Seterusnya Salahuddin berkata (ini bagi saya amat menarik): "Bukankah ini jelas menunjukkan rasuah yang dipersepsikan berlaku ketika itu turut ditolak oleh orang Melayu?" Oleh itu saya pelik. Jika tahu rakyat termasuk orang Melayu tolak rasuah mengapa Umno terus-menerus mempertahankan pemimpin yang dilihat ramai sebagai perasuah?

Dengan menggunakan istilah 'persepsi', Umno masih anggap Najib tidak melakukan rasuah meskipun Mahkamah Tinggi, Mahkamah Rayuan, dan Mahkamah Persekutuan -- membabitkan sembilan hakim -- mendapati dia bersalah dalam kes SRC International.

Bak kata wartawan veteran, A Kadir Jasin, di Facebook tempoh hari. "Ada pemimpin, ahli dan penyokong Umno yang gembira teramat sangat dengan pengampunan diraja. Ada yang gembira hingga lupa diri, tetapi ada juga yang sedar bahawa pengampunan bekas presiden mereka menyukarkan pemulihan parti tersebut."

Kata Kadir, dalam kalangan pemimpin dan ahli Umno ada yang tidak peduli sangat dengan hal-hal bersangkutan undang-undang, moral dan harga diri. "Bagi mereka skandal penyonglapan duit 1MDB bukanlah isu besar."

Menurut Kadir, "yang rugi dalam saga ini, adalah rakyat jelata dan pembayar cukai. Untuk membayar balik hutang 1MDB sahaja sebanyak RM42.5 bilion duit awam telah dibelanjakan sehingga 30 Jun ini. Pada ketika rakyat jelata yang tidak bersalah dibebankan dengan berbilion-bilion duit 1MDB yang dicuri dan pelbagai kemelut ekonomi, pihak-pihak yang membuat angkara semakin dimanjakan."

Memang benar kata Kadir. Lantas saya ulangi apa yang saya sering nyatakan pada beberapa penulisan sebelum ini. Selagi Umno mempertahankan Najib selagi itulah rakyat termasuk orang Melayu akan terus menjauhi Umno. Meminjam kata-kata Kadir tadi "menyukarkan pemulihan parti tersebut".
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
a79c88e08945a934: It was about time someone from the red half of Manchester piped up.
The sound from the noisy neighbours has drowned out any criticism of its own bungling.
Nothing like the hanging offences of their counterparts at City, but still enough to merit a stern reprimand from long-suffering fans.
Lisandro Martinez spoke for much of United’s diaspora when he let his frustration pour out after a 2-0 Champions League defeat at Atletico Madrid.
This was not another Brighton or Grimsby moment – there was no great shame in losing to one of Europe’s top sides in their own den and ultimately with 10 men.
But it was another failure, and United have had only two successes in nine games this season – against newly promoted Ipswich and Azerbaijani minnows, Sabah.
Next up is their historic nemesis Leeds in another ‘cauldron of hate’ at Elland Road, a tough place to go at the best of times.
On a roll and aware of the rivalry, Daniel Farke’s men will be primed for the kill. The Damned United indeed.
It’s another of the fixture list’s “last place they would want to go to” assignments, but hardly what City faced at Anfield.
Whether United can rally as City did to rise above it is doubtful – their players are just not in the same class.
Nor will they have the same level of motivation.
Those in the dressing room who take umbrage at not being deemed good enough might, but many will surely agree with the Argentina defender.
Michael Carrick may, too.
Damned by faint praise – “he does his best” – Carrick got off lightly compared to those “in other areas”, especially technical director Jason Wilcox.
But Carrick will know that there has to be a reaction from “the Politburo” besides a routine fine for Martinez.
He will also know that, unlike when Ruben Amorim was given the benefit of the doubt, there are big names after his job.
Favourite is Eddie Howe, who thought he was building something big at Newcastle until the owners sold his best players.
Second favourite is Antonio Conte, whose CV is littered with league titles (including the EPL at Chelsea), but also bust-ups, short tenures and dismal failures in Europe.
You’d expect co-owner Jim Ratcliffe to go for Steady Eddie over the combustible Italian, exciting though it may be.
But both would demand substantial budgets for the rebuild.
Intriguingly, Conte isn’t the only Italian on the list: the other is Carlo Ancelotti.
A long shot, but if he decides he’s been dealt a poor hand of Brazilian players, he could be tempted.
Ratcliffe would like him, but can he afford him? Are there any more tea-ladies at Old Trafford left to sack?
The wise money is surely on him waiting to see if Carrick can turn it around.
And you’d like to think he knows it’s not the manager’s fault – Martinez is right, it’s “in other areas”.
The crackpot recruitment idea of focusing on one part of the field per season is no longer a laughing matter.
But what is amusing is that after insisting he wouldn’t pay “silly money”, Ratcliffe did just that.
Returning to Europe’s top competition was something to build on and United rewarded Carrick for steadying the listing ship with a permanent job and long-term contract.
But instead of going for the leading names available, United refused to pay the admittedly steep asking prices.
For Elliot Anderson, City paid Forest £116m, while Southampton persuaded Spurs to shed £85m for Mateus Fernandes, whom United had long courted.
So United settled for two players well down their list.
Youri Tielemans, at the end of his contract with Aston Villa, represented decent value at £35m.
But Chelsea’s Brazilian youngster, Andrey Santos at £50m, seemed just the sort of price Ratcliffe said he wouldn’t pay.
So, too, Carlos Baleba, a long-term target for whom Brighton extracted £70m.
The Cameroonian has hardly played after injury, but for a total of £155m, United are well short of transforming their squad.
However you look at it, the strategy was dumb, poorly executed and ended in panic.
Once the budget was spent, there was still a glaring gap at left-back and no second striker.
Luke Shaw is 31 and creaking and has no replacement. Perhaps if Howe comes, he can persuade Lewis Hall to join him.
United refused to pay Newcastle’s asking price, which has no doubt risen after Hall’s England form, but were fleeced by Chelsea for Santos in a position in which they’d already covered.
Baleba may be the best, but they couldn’t avoid paying the “Brighton tax”.
For a club returning to the Champions League, £155m was a paltry amount to invest – incredibly on three players in the same position.
They were even outspent by promoted clubs, who took the trouble to bolster other areas of their squads.
Someone could also have told United that recruiting from within the EPL is not the way to get value (Tielemans excepted).
But it’s not just in players where Wilcox’s judgement is being questioned.
After arriving from Southampton in 2024, he pushed strongly to retain both Erik ten Hag (after an eighth-place finish) and Amorim after United ended 15th.
And they lost the Europa League final to Tottenham, too.
What Wilcox cannot be blamed for is if the prodigy, JJ Gabriel, to whom United are still clinging, ends up leaving. That may have more to do with pushy parenting than any slackness by the club.
But it’s a grim picture that someone had to highlight. That it came from within the dressing room makes a response more urgent.
Meanwhile, the silence from the Glazers, the majority owners, is thundering.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
d59b82c0813934bf: Marking the 30th anniversary of KDE on October 14, the project released Plasma 6.8, debuted a movie, and retired Plasma's native X11 session support. The announcement from KDE dubs the new Plasma 6.8 as the "30th Anniversary Edition" and describes the update as preparing Plasma for the future. Legacy X11 applications will still function via the XWayland compatibility layer, and KDE applications will also continue supporting X11 under other desktop environments.

After 42 years in service, the X11 protocol is losing another major desktop environment. Plasma will fully adopt the Wayland system and put support for starting new X11 sessions in Plasma to bed. Users opting to stay on Plasma 6.7 will keep their existing sessions for now. The move was expected, with GNOME officially dropping X11 sessions by default in 2025.

The new Plasma 6.8 brings many improvements, including increased support for adding window decorations (like shadows and rounded corners) to third-party apps, and a more streamlined Union theming system. Other notable additions include Nvidia triple buffering being enabled by default, Kup backup integration (KDE's backup utility—now integrated into Plasma), and kscreenctl, a command-line utility that allows power users to adjust display configurations.
ae01081f072dc8d6: Plex, which made a name for itself by letting users share movies they own, is now helping sell movie theater tickets. The company is looking to monetize its content-discovery capabilities and expand its business beyond its media server software.
Plex partnered with Fandango, which has sold movie tickets since 2000, to drive ticket sales from people searching for movies to stream. Per the announcement:

Starting today, Plex users in the US will see a Fandango ticketing option on title pages for movies currently playing in theaters, allowing them to click through to Fandango to find showtimes and purchase tickets. The integration also enables direct attribution through Kochava, giving studios and advertisers greater visibility into how campaigns and audience engagement translate into ticket sales.

Fandango says it sells tickets for 31,000 movie theater screens in the US. The Plex deal allows it to leverage data from Plex’s streaming service (Plex claims users of the service “make more than 100 million streaming decisions each month”), including "ratings and cross-platform viewing" to gain “insight into audience intent," the announcement said.
714b79603cd0b3ac: Up to a quarter of active-duty Army members could receive a low testosterone result from mandatory military screening, despite the true prevalence of the condition likely being a tiny fraction of that figure, according to a study published Thursday in JAMA.

The finding adds to concerns that the mandatory screening announced by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in July will lead to a cascade of unnecessary medical evaluations for military members. Those evaluations could result in inappropriate testing, inaccurate results and diagnoses, and overtreatment that could cause harm, including infertility. Medical experts, including the Endocrine Society and the American Urological Association (AUA), have recommended against blanket screenings for these reasons. Still, the Pentagon has moved forward with the plans, releasing clinical guidance in September.

The JAMA study highlights the reasons why testosterone levels are not measured in men without symptoms—and also offers a glimpse of how many Army members could become ensnared in the clinically dubious screenings.
e2eb449edbb77f0a: When corporate leaders discuss climate strategy, the message that still dominates is that, despite competing priorities and external pressures, sustainability matters.  According to the 2026 State of Supply Chain Sustainability Report from the MIT Sustainable Supply Chain Lab, which surveyed 1,810 supply chain professionals across 91 countries, 83 percent rate sustainability as important or very important to long-term business success, the highest level in the report's seven-year history. But commitment, the report reveals, is not the same as capacity. While 59 percent of respondents report becoming more committed to sustainability following recent U.S. policy shifts that deprioritize environmental concerns, the same organizations are being forced to compromise those commitments. Sixty-eight percent report that tariff uncertainty has compelled them to delay, scale back, or abandon sustainability strategies. Nearly one-third have seen tariff-related disruptions actually increase their operational emissions. "Commitment is strong, measurement is expanding, and AI is accelerating," says Sreedevi Rajagopalan, director of the MIT Sustainable Supply Chain Lab and lead author of the report. "What comes next is harder: converting commitment into accountability, operational integration into strategic decision-making, and incremental decarbonization into genuine transition." The result is a supply chain sustainability agenda stuck between conviction and constraint.  Beyond tariffs, more than eight in 10 respondents across North America, Europe, and Asia agree that ongoing geopolitical conflict is reducing the effectiveness of their organization’s climate action. Organizations built decarbonization plans on assumptions of stable trade and relative peace, yet neither assumption is holding. The external disruption reveals an internal vulnerability. Among companies with publicly stated sustainability goals, only 51 percent have established a formal cross-functional sustainability team, which is the governance structure most strongly associated with embedding sustainability into daily decisions. In addition, only 33 percent place sustainability oversight at the board level. Public ambition, in other words, is vastly outrunning internal accountability infrastructure. Companies with formal cross-functional teams report sustainability is "frequently or always" built into decisions 57 percent of the time. Where responsibility sits in a single function, that drops to 13 percent — a 44-point gap illustrating the return on governance investment. Sustainability is embedding most deeply where companies make daily operational choices: transportation and logistics (39 percent), procurement (35 percent), warehousing (34 percent), and product design (33 percent). However, it thins out dramatically in decisions that lock in long-term emissions: capital investment, network design, and supply chain risk planning. This reveals that companies are becoming better at operating more sustainably, but not at designing sustainable supply chains in the long term. The artificial intelligence story compounds this tension. Seventy-eight percent of North American organizations report current use of AI in sustainability initiatives, and 87 percent of adopters report positive impact on sustainability goals. Eighty-six percent have reduced material waste, 81 percent have reduced energy use, and 63 percent use AI to estimate missing supplier emissions data. However, among mature agentic AI users, only 53 percent report a reduction in total greenhouse gas emissions. Twenty-nine percent report an increase, suggesting that operational efficiency does not automatically translate into lower net emissions. This tension is particularly visible in warehousing. Among advanced and fully automated warehouses using AI, 78 percent report higher energy use since implementing AI, and 76 percent report higher waste, yet only 24 percent use AI-driven real-time monitoring to track environmental consequences. Many organizations may not realize their energy footprint is climbing until well after implementation. Another key area of the report is freight transportation. Nearly every freight company is reducing emissions through route optimization, load consolidation, and driver-behavior programs. However, 43 percent of fleets still operate mostly or entirely on conventional diesel and only 8 percent have completed a full transition to low-emission energy. The divergence between regions reveals why: In Europe, 84 percent of freight companies report that recent policy changes have positively affected decarbonization strategy. In North America, only 44 percent do. When policy signals are unclear, capital-intensive technology transitions stall. For example, battery-electric vehicles are at scale in 60 percent of European companies, but only 36 percent in North America. The report reveals that one bright spot has emerged in Scope 3, or indirect, emissions collaboration. Participation in joint supplier engagement and decarbonization programs surged from 31 to 58 percent in a single year. In addition, partnerships to manage shared suppliers' emissions more than doubled, from 23 to 55 percent. The share working entirely alone collapsed from 18 to 6 percent. The report, supported by the C.H. Robinson Foundation, Breakthrough, and CO2 AI and Dassault Systèmes, reveals that companies are recognizing that Scope 3 cannot be solved in isolation.  Across all these areas, the consistent pattern the report reveals is that corporate commitment is not the prevailing constraint to ongoing sustainability efforts. Rather, governance, accountability structures, technology infrastructure, and measurement capabilities are the current obstacles. Organizations that close the external gap by building resilience against disruption and the internal gap by hard-wiring accountability into structure will be the ones whose commitments survive. Those that do not will find that ambition without accountability moves the needle very little.
c0a2e19f9297635f: As an embryo develops from a small cluster of stem cells, those once “blank slate” cells begin to take on more specialized roles like brain, liver, or muscle cells, and organize themselves into three-dimensional structures such as tissues and organs. The fate of each cell — what type of specialized cell it will become — depends on which genes are turned on or off in the cell. These patterns of gene activity shape the cell’s structure and function, enabling it to take on a specific role in the body. But this decision isn’t up to individual cells. They constantly send and receive chemical signals to and from neighboring cells, which help them understand where they are, what stage of development they are in, and what they should become. These messages spread through multi-step sequences called signaling pathways, which translate external signals into specific changes in gene activity in the cell. For researchers, being able to retrace the sequence of instructions a cell has received would offer a powerful way to understand how tissues develop and how these processes go awry in disease.  But this has been difficult to achieve because scientists have long assumed that the effects of signaling pathways vary widely across cell types, meaning they would need to map each pathway separately in each cell type — an arduous and painstaking process. Now, in a new study led by MIT assistant professor of biology and Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research member Pulin Li and graduate student Nicholas Hutchins, researchers have discovered that each signaling pathway leaves behind a unique “fingerprint” — a distinctive pattern of gene activity that reflects the particular signals the cell has encountered. Importantly, these fingerprints are consistent across different cell types for the same signaling pathway, which means that instead of mapping each cell type separately, scientists can reconstruct signaling histories across many cell types using these pathway-specific fingerprints. This discovery was made possible through a machine learning model called IRIS. This model can detect fingerprints of different signaling pathways and pinpoint which signals a cell received at different stages of development inside an embryo, even for cell types it hasn’t encountered before.  This artificial intelligence-driven approach marks a major advance over traditional methods, which require researchers to experimentally test every pathway in every possible cell type, and opens up the possibility to comprehensively map the signaling histories of every cell inside a mouse or human embryo at an unprecedented scale. “Think of voice recognition systems like Siri, which are trained mainly in English, but then use that training to help them recognize other languages,” says Li. “This is called transfer learning, and this is why IRIS can work across many different cell types.” The researchers’ detailed open-access findings, published in the journal Nature Methods on Sept. 8, could accelerate stem cell engineering for regenerative medicine and improve the creation of organoids — miniature, 3D models that mimic real organs — for studying disease mechanisms and testing new drugs. This is because once researchers learn the pattern of signals that drives a stem cell to become a specific cell type, they can recreate those signals to control the fate of stem cells in a lab or medical setting. IRIS is a neural network-based model, which, in essence, is an AI-driven system designed to recognize patterns in complex data, similar to how our brains spot patterns. It examines a cell’s overall gene activity and estimates which signaling pathways were likely “on” at specific times during development. Li and Hutchins trained IRIS on a large experimental dataset that measured how thousands of human embryonic stem cells responded to dozens of combinations of six major signaling pathways at multiple stages of development. This created a comprehensive map, or atlas, of how signaling combinations influence cell behavior.  The team then tested IRIS using single cells from mouse embryos during gastrulation, a stage when cells are rapidly branching into different fates. IRIS could accurately predict when and where specific signaling pathways would activate in cells destined to become part of heart, gut, muscle, and spinal cord tissue. This variation in signaling molecules is what guides cells to form the right structures in the right places. With this approach, scientists can not only begin to understand the fundamentals of cell-to-cell communication, but also gain a practical roadmap for guiding stem cells into specific, functional cell types in the lab. When the researchers employed IRIS to identify signals needed to create a cell type critical for lung development, the model predicted that activating a specific signaling pathway would encourage lung-specific development. Experiments in mouse embryos confirmed the model’s prediction. By identifying the precise combinations of signals that drive lung cell development, they can more reliably generate accurate, lab-grown models of lung tissue. “In these ways, IRIS is helping us decode the language cells use to talk to each other at a much faster rate than we could realistically achieve through experiments,” Hutchins says. These improved models would allow researchers to study diseases like asthma, lung cancer, and pulmonary fibrosis, in which lung tissue becomes scarred, often without a known cause. They can then use these models to test potential therapies, and ultimately design regenerative treatments that can repair the damaged tissue.

70c732a9a0197878: In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant possible.

Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about nuclear power plants trying to do just that. Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. And on October 5, the Department of Energy awarded a $4.2 billion loan to Vistra for previously announced upgrades at three plants.
Pushing existing reactors to produce more could help provide more clean power for data centers, quickly. But just how much additional power can we count on?

Upgrading equipment at existing nuclear power plants can allow them to reach a higher capacity; the process is called a power uprate. Operators have been doing this since the 1970s in the US, but it’s been less common in recent years as demand for electricity plateaued and cheap natural gas put financial pressure on nuclear power plants. Some plants closed, and putting in more money to produce more electricity didn’t make much sense at others. Between 2001 and 2010, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved over 80 uprates. Between 2011 and 2020, the number was 33.

But with the rise of AI and the related boom in electricity demand, there’s been a shift. We’re seeing shuttered plants like Palisades and Three Mile Island race to reopen. And existing plants are looking to uprate again.

Some uprates are minor, involving changes to instrument setpoints or calculations at the plant. But more major overhauls, which can boost reactor power by as much as 20%, require replacing plant equipment.

Generally, uprates involve using fuel that’s more highly enriched, or a higher volume of fresh fuel, in the nuclear reactor. That helps produce more steam, which is used to turn a turbine and generate electricity. To handle that additional energy, the main turbines and equipment such as pumps, motors, generators, and transformers are upgraded.

The most recent major uprate approved in the US was for three reactors at the Browns Ferry nuclear power plant in Alabama. A $475 million project saw that plant expand its power capacity by 14% between 2018 and 2019.

Things could pick up soon, though. Constellation announced plans this week to spend more than $4.3 billion on uprates to 11 reactors. The additional electricity will be enough to power roughly 700,000 US homes.

Behind it all? Big Tech money. Google agreed to buy electricity from these plants, and the 20-year agreement was a major factor in making the uprates happen. As Joe Dominguez, Constellation’s CEO, told the New York Times: “These are capital intensive, labor intensive projects that require a different price point than the market trades at, frankly.”

Also in the last few weeks, the US Department of Energy shared that it will commit over $4 billion to help finance upgrades and modernization for Vistra nuclear power plants across Pennsylvania and Ohio. Those projects will add 433 megawatts of power capacity, and Meta has already signed on to buy electricity from the plants in a long-term deal.

A note about cost: On a per-kilowatt basis, that Constellation project is less expensive than building a new reactor, but it’s still more expensive than building a new utility-scale solar farm with energy storage or a combined-cycle natural-gas plant.

Even at this high cost, uprates are in high demand. Today, the US nuclear fleet has roughly 98 gigawatts of total power capacity. Depending on who you ask, there’s somewhere between three and eight additional gigawatts on the table from uprates. A pretty significant chunk of the potential uprates in the US are already accounted for—the NRC already expects applications to add 2.4 gigawatts of power to reactors through 2032.

It’s crucial to put these plans (and the total potential for uprates in the US) in perspective, though. PJM, the grid operator that covers much of the East Coast, expects about 30 gigawatts of additional peak demand because of AI by 2030. All the possible nationwide nuclear uprates would cover just a fraction of that.

Making the most of existing nuclear reactors is a relatively easy win at a time when we need all the zero-emissions power we can get. But there’s still a lot of demand, and if we want more nuclear power to meet it, eventually that will require actually building new reactors.

cfb3c2ddc081661a: Have you ever thought about what makes you you? Science assures us it has everything to do with the three-pound organ between our ears, with its billions of neurons and trillions of delicate connections. But it’s a lot trickier to explain why we have a sense of self-awareness or to pin down precisely where that first memory of Mommy actually resides. As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.

To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going—even beyond death. Let’s call them the “mind savers.” They’re exploring everything from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones to uploading our memories to the cloud. Here, we look at six possible paths for keeping your mind going, how feasible they’d be, and what benefits the ­present-day research might bring—even if cognitive immortality doesn’t pan out.
EDDIE GUY
Head transplant

White’s experiments have been a source of grim fascination ever since. But to a few neuroscientists they’re inspiration, suggesting that one day a human head transplant—or, as some call it, a body transplant—could succeed.

The idea’s main proponent is Sergio Canavero, a controversial Italian surgeon who, 10 years ago, even claimed he’d found a volunteer in Valery Spiridinov, a computer programmer suffering from a degenerative muscle disease. Spiridinov initially agreed to have his head transferred to the body of a brain-dead donor in China, but he later bowed out of the plan and instead got married. And that might be just as well. Critics say the procedure would be more like murder than medicine. Or, best-case scenario: Volunteers would be left paralyzed and in need of a ventilator for life.

Canavero says that’s not necessarily true. He claims people’s views on the operation will change once they accept that reconnecting severed spinal cords is already possible. He pointed MIT Technology Review to a research article from this past summer that he coauthored with surgeons at Moscow’s Sklifosovsky Research and Clinical Institute for Emergency Medicine. The team cut through the spinal cords of three pigs at a point midway along their backs and then tested whether the severed nerve bodies could be fused back together using a surgical sealant. According to that paper, which appeared in the journal PLOS One, all the pigs regained the ability to stand and even walk unsteadily.

Does that mean a head could be attached to a new body and then actually control it? Mainstream researchers aren’t convinced. Grégoire Courtine, a spinal rehabilitation specialist at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne in Switzerland, says he’s been following Canavero’s claims “with little respect” and thinks that we should “pay zero attention.”
“There is no technology … capable of such a crazy idea,” Courtine wrote in an email.
Mindclones

Just 12 years after the book came out, artificial-intelligence technology has already brought some of her predictions to “life,” so to speak. Services such as StoryFile, Afterlife AI, and Synthesia allow users to upload their personal information and likeness in order to produce either conversational bots that share their memories or video talking heads that sound (and look) exactly like them. Influencers now let their “AI clones” do their work on TikTok, and some people are even building avatars of their aging parents in order to preserve their personalities.

While this mimicry can produce comical results, unhealthy attachments, or uncanny vibes, the increasing realism of generative AI invites people to emotionally accept the avatars as real beings. That was the case when Rothblatt appeared as a digital avatar during a 2025 event held by the UCLA Department of Communication called “The Bridge to Humanizing AI.”

Her copy, named Marvatar, was projected on a screen, led the discussions, and talked with the meatspace Rothblatt as an equal, at one point saying, “The dance isn’t about who leads, but how we move together.” According to the university, attendees were “visibly moved” and wept “with wonder” at Rothblatt’s vision of digital equality.

What’s still missing from Rothblatt’s mindclone prediction is evidence that these avatars have—or ever will have—any kind of true self-awareness. (We asked ChatGPT if it’s conscious, and it answered, “Probably not.”) But all that remains a gray zone. Neuroscientists don’t have a clear definition of consciousness, much less a diagnostic test they could apply to an avatar.
Instead, what if the final determination is in the eye of the beholder? Your digital clone might not be you. But at some point it might be good enough for me.
Brain in a jar

So, campy sci-fi film lovers that we are, it got our attention last year when a company called Bexorg started showing journalists actual human brains in vats, which it has been acquiring from organ donors soon after death and then “rebooting” by infusing them with oxygen-rich artificial blood.

The company claims these “physiologically intact human brains” will be more useful than animals for drug testing and safer than trying experiments on living volunteers. Add an Alzheimer’s compound to one of these disembodied brains and researchers can then measure exactly what the drug does inside the organ.

Bexorg’s CEO, Zvonimir Vrselja, is “sure” that some people would like to restore consciousness to out-of-body brains, but he’s tried to douse such speculation. While they are metabolically active, the company says, the brains have lost all coordinated electrical activity. That means they aren’t conscious—although, just to make sure, the neuroscientists running the experiments add the strong anesthetic propofol to the tissues.

What’s more, right now a brain can be kept “alive” outside the body for only about 24 hours. That wouldn’t be much of a second life. Still, efforts are underway to improve the life-support systems. Bexorg says it hopes to eventually keep its brains going for two weeks.
EDDIE GUY
Gradual brain replacement

On paper, the goal is to manufacture tissue to graft into the brains of stroke victims, reversing damage and restoring function. Less officially, the project’s existence is a surprise coup for an extreme plan to defeat aging advanced by Jean Hébert, the neuroscientist leading the program, who argued in his 2020 book, Replacing Aging, that we can live longer by replacing our aging brain cells with young ones.
We don’t want to lose our identities. That’s why—according to Hébert—it would have to happen gradually, in small chunks, so our brains would have time to adapt to the new tissue.

Scientists who applied for the program say Hébert insisted on a very specific technological approach. While most researchers engineer individual cell types, ARPA-H asked for complex chunks of young, functional cortex—more or less like what you’d find in a developing fetus. “He wanted to create essentially an embryonic form of cortex that he thought you could somehow graft into an adult brain,” says Marius Wernig, a Stanford University stem-cell researcher who applied.

Skeptics say it’s unknown whether replacement brain chunks will ever properly function as part of your brain—say, by taking over memories. What’s more, it’s still unclear how to manufacture youthful cortex, or what ARPA-H calls “neocortical precursor tissue,” in the lab. One idea is to employ the latest advances in brain organoids. Imagine, if you will, a human cortex grown in a lab dish without a body.

We know that the agency has an aggressive timeline: Over the course of five years, it wants researchers to lay the foundation for the first human tests of replacement cortex. The aim, it says, is to “take the ‘permanent’ out of brain damage.” And maybe out of old age, too.
Brain upload

Scientists are already mapping this wiring in simpler animals. Two years ago, Seung took part in analyzing a fly brain that had been cut into paper-thin sheets and imaged with an electron microscope. Then he and his colleagues used image-analysis software to trace 139,255 neurons and about 55 million synapses. The fly map could lead to energy-efficient software that computes the way real brains do, Seung says.

Others believe the ultimate outcome of “connectomics” research will be what’s called “whole-brain emulation,” or sometimes just “uploading.” It’s the idea, popular in some quarters of Silicon Valley, that a simulation created from a sliced-up brain could become so detailed that it would reproduce not only a generic intelligence but a particular one, like yours—complete with memories and opinions, and able to live again in a data server somewhere.

Setting aside the question of whether a simulation would really be you, everyone agrees that this technology isn’t coming in time for those of us alive today. A survey of 312 neuroscientists, published in 2025 in PLOS One, estimated that human whole-brain emulation wouldn’t happen before 2125.

That long and unpredictable tech horizon helps explain why two US companies, Nectome and Sparks Brain Preservation, are offering to preserve human brains (or bodies) today by infusing them with the same potent chemicals used to “fix” the brains of fruit flies for connectome mapping. The idea: If the fine details of a brain’s structure can be preserved, one day in the far future it might be reanimated.

But there’s a startling twist. Because brain tissue needs to be preserved quickly after a person’s death, both companies say they want to work with people taking advantage of medical aid in dying, now legal in 13 states and Washington, DC. In that procedure, doctors supply a lethal dose of drugs, but it’s the patient—someone with a terminal prognosis—who pushes the plunger. For a fee, the companies say, they can have a preservation team at the ready. So far, the service is not popular. The companies each say they are still awaiting their first aid-in-dying customer.
EDDIE GUY
Synthetic neocortex
That’s right: an extra brain.

Recently, we’ve seen inklings of how this might come to pass. In 2024, Science Corporation, in California, unveiled a “biohybrid” brain-computer interface featuring nerve cells grown on a digital chip. Placed on an animal’s brain, these cells sent out long, thin axons that integrated with the animal’s own neurons. The result: two-way communication from computer to brain, in the brain’s language.

The technology could permit new types of medicine, like an implant that directs brain cells to produce dopamine and thereby treat Parkinson’s. But Max Hodak, the company’s CEO, says it also might count as a new brain part, which he likens to a “big, externalized cranial nerve.”

Such a device could serve as the connector to Kurzweil’s computerized neocortex in the cloud, giving a living person unlimited extra processing power. Still other entrepreneurs believe if you kept adding biohybrid components to a brain, eventually you could morph it into an immortal machine.

Daniel Burger, founder of the venture-­funded stealth startup Eightsix Science (its name refers to the 86 billion neurons in a human brain), says this dream could require mixing several of the brain-saving techniques on this list. He thinks we might need brains in vats, affording neuro-­engineers easy access, so they can gradually replace brain parts with biohybrid neural grafts.

The ultimate goal is to migrate your mind into your extra, engineered brain, without ever breaking the continuity of self. “It’s not the typical ‘scan, store, simulate,’” says Burger. “I don’t think simulations will be conscious.” He adds, “We’re saying it’s going to be way more complicated, and it’s probably going to look like gradual brain replacement into a hardware brain.”

Once your mind is hardware, you won’t need a biological body. Instead, you could take up residence in a data center somewhere and perhaps even have backups distributed around the globe. “From that point on,” Burger acknowledges, “stuff becomes really crazy.”
bb8da7cf13f68595: Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists. They hope to replicate the findings with human organs.

The kidneys—which are similar in size to human ones—were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working.

“Ten years ago … I wouldn’t say I had high hopes it was actually going to work,” says Erik Finger, a transplant surgeon at the University of Minnesota who co-led the work. “After we did the last transplant, I walked out of the room and said, ‘This is a big deal.’” The research was shared at the preprint server bioRxiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed.
The kidneys aren’t perfect, and the researchers have yet to demonstrate that they can sustain life over the long term. But the results represent a milestone achievement, say others in the field.

“Thank God that someone’s actually managed to do it in one organ and prove that it works,” says Peter Kilbride, a cryobiologist and cofounder of Kyros Kairos, a company focused on improving funding for cryopreservation research, who was not involved in the research. “For years, people have been trying and failing to get to this step. Finally, we’ve got this breakthrough.”

“Their work is amazing and will enable us to truly, indefinitely bank organs,” says Korkut Uygun, a biomedical engineer and professor of surgery at Harvard Medical School, who was also not involved in the research. “It is a revolutionary time for transplantation.”
Buying time

Every year, tens of thousands of organ transplants take place in the US alone. These procedures are thought to have saved 2 million years of life in the last 25 years. But there’s plenty of room for improvement.

One major challenge is the lack of available organs. Even when an organ becomes available, it can be difficult to get it to the right recipient within 24 to 36 hours, which is the current limit for preserving human organs.

People who receive organ transplants must also take drugs that suppress their immune systems for the rest of their lives. These drugs are meant to stop their bodies from rejecting the new organs. But they come with side effects and increase the risk of infections and cancer.

The ability to bank organs for long periods of time holds the promise to address all these challenges. Doctors would have more time to match organs to recipients. They’d be able to limit the risk of organ rejection, too—potentially by preparing recipients, and their immune systems, beforehand.
“With real organ banking … instead of the patients waiting for the organ, it’s the organs that are waiting for the patients,” says Finger.

Scientists have been able to cool cells to ultra-low temperatures through a process called vitrification, which essentially turns them to something like glass. This procedure is already used to store eggs, sperm, and embryos. Vitrifying whole organs is much harder.

Some problems can be avoided with cryoprotectants—chemicals that work like antifreeze and prevent damaging ice crystals from forming. But these chemicals tend to be incredibly toxic. It’s also difficult to rapidly and uniformly cool large tissues, and just as hard to evenly rewarm an organ all the way through.

Working with John Bischof, a bioengineer at the University of Minnesota, Finger and colleagues have come up with a solution. Once an organ has been loaded with a cryoprotectant, they infuse it with iron oxide nanoparticles. These nanoparticles don’t do anything to the cells. But when it’s time to rewarm the organ, they can be activated with an electromagnetic field.

When the radiofrequency of that field switches between two states, the particles also flip, realigning themselves with the field. That causes them to release heat throughout the organ. Adjusting the power of the field allows the team to control the rate of heating so that it gets faster once the organ reaches -120°C.

The researchers successfully vitrified rat kidneys using this approach in work published in 2023. Back then, they were able to rewarm kidneys that had been kept in a freezer for up to 100 days before transplanting them into rats.

Since then, the team has been trying to achieve the same success with bigger organs. Pig kidneys are thought to be a good model for human ones—they’re about the same size and look similar. Rat kidneys weigh around one gram; pig kidneys are around 100.

It hasn’t been easy. The cryoprotectant used for vitrifying rat kidneys didn’t work as well in the pig organs. “We had to rediscover and modify the cocktail,” says Bischof. “That’s why it’s taken us three years.”
Deep-freezing kidneys

The first step in the procedure is to remove a kidney from a donor pig. Once it’s out, the kidney is flushed with a commonly used organ preservation solution to remove the blood, bagged, and temporarily laid on a bed of ice in a cooler so it can be taken over to the engineering lab.

There, team members unpack the kidney and hook it up to a device they’ve designed to control the organ’s temperature and pressure. Then they start to load it up with the cocktail of cryoprotectants, slowly enough to ensure an even spread through the organ but quickly enough to minimize any toxic effects. It takes around two hours.

The next step is to infuse the organ with the iron oxide nanoparticles, which are pumped through the organ for around seven to eight minutes, says Finger. Then it’s time to cool the organ by pumping cold nitrogen vapor into a chamber housing it.

It’s a delicate process, and the team must ensure that the organ is cooling all the way through. At the same time, they must lower the kidney’s temperature as quickly as possible to prevent ice from forming. “Oftentimes there are multiple people doing different things to make sure that things don’t go awry,” says Bischof.

Once the organ reaches the vitrified state at around -120 °C, it “behaves like a glass,” says Finger. “At that point, you can stay stable for long periods of time—we think indefinitely.” The team then pauses the cooling process to ensure that the organ is glassy throughout. Otherwise, it could crack.

After the pause, if everything goes well, the kidney is ultimately cooled to -150 °C. Once it’s in the freezer, it can stay there for days, weeks, or even months. The team has kept a small number of kidneys banked for over a year.
Pink right up

The real test of these kidneys comes when they’re taken out of the freezer, rewarmed, and flushed of their chemicals and nanoparticles. Can they support life? So far, the team has tested some of them in a couple of different ways.

In one set of experiments, the researchers put rewarmed kidneys on perfusion devices—systems that are already used in transplant surgeries both to provide organs with nutrients and to help doctors assess them while they’re out of the body.

In another set of experiments, Finger and his colleagues transplanted rewarmed kidneys into pigs and monitored them for two hours. In both experiments, the rewarmed kidneys seemed to recover, says Finger. “They pink right up,” he says.
COURTESY OF THE RESEARCHERS

There are lots of ways to measure the function of a kidney, but one key test is whether or not the organ can make urine. By this measure, the rewarmed kidneys did well, although they produced around two-thirds of the amount that would normally be expected. “They produce urine … within a minute or so,” says Finger. “We know that they work.”

Most of the rewarmed kidneys had been banked for days or weeks. But one had been in the freezer for just over a year. When Finger and his colleagues rewarmed it and put it on a perfusion machine, they found that it produced urine “immediately.” “It actually looked better than many of the [other] kidneys,” says Finger. “We’re comfortable now saying we can store them for a year and rewarm them with excellent function.”

“It’s a very big deal to go a year,” says Kevin Myer, president and CEO of LifeGift, an organ procurement organization based in Texas. Being able to store organs for that length of time would transform organ transplantation. He envisions banks of organs that could be used on demand in emergency cases where people can’t wait, such as for some drug overdoses or gunshot wounds.
Final hurdles

But the procedure isn’t ready for prime time just yet. As well as producing less urine than expected, the rewarmed kidneys also showed signs of injury. The damage seems to be caused by the cryoprotectant chemicals, say the researchers.
“This is one big breakthrough that solves half the problem,” as Kilbride puts it.

The team has shown that the rewarmed kidneys can regain blood flow, which is “very important,” says Greg Fahy, a cryobiologist who is considered a pioneer in the field. But he’s worried about the extent of the damage to the organs. “We can’t tell from these experiments whether these kidneys might have supported life or not.”

But Fahy, who is chief scientific officer at the biotech companies Intervene Immune and 21st Century Medicine (where he is also executive director), acknowledges that it’s not clear how these kidneys might fare once they’re inside a living animal for the long term.

Finger also hopes to find ways to repair the damage seen in the kidneys. Other research has shown that the health of transplant organs can improve while they’re on perfusion machines. And damaged kidneys might undergo some level of self-repair once they’re in a body. At any rate, human kidneys may cope better with the process than pig kidneys, says Finger.

The next step will be to test the kidneys in pigs over longer periods of time. The team, along with many other researchers in the field, will continue the search for less toxic cryoprotectants, too. Finger, Bischof, and their colleagues are also planning experiments with human kidneys.

Finger is optimistic. “We’re going to see that there’s injury, and it’s not perfect … but now we’ve got to the point where it works,” he says. “These are big, historic milestones in our field, and we’re excited about it.”
548342f77b75d402: From Lim Teck Ghee
In Selangor, a voter in Sabak Bernam has roughly six times as much say in who goes to Parliament as a voter in Bangi. Nationally, the largest seat has about 10 times the voters of the smallest.
That is not "one person, one vote".

This can be fixed before the next general election (GE16) without amending the Federal Constitution and without any state losing a single seat. The window is open now. The eight-year constitutional freeze on redrawing peninsula boundaries ended in March 2026, and the Sabah and Sarawak freezes have also lapsed.
But the clock is short: every step must be completed before Parliament is dissolved for GE16. If it is not, the next election will be fought on the 2018 map.
At a glance

The problem: some voters' ballots carry six times as much weight as others', even within the same state. The fix: redraw boundaries so no seat is more than one-third above or below its state's average.

What it needs: a simple majority in the Dewan Rakyat. No constitutional amendment. No state loses a seat. The deadline: the report must be passed before Parliament dissolves, no later than Dec 19, 2027.
There are more than 300,000 voters in Bangi, Selangor. There are about 51,000 voters in Sabak Bernam in the same state. There is a 6:1 value difference between their vote power.

Population growth, urban migration and the Undi18 reforms – automatic voter registration and lowering the voting age to 18 – added millions of new voters, many in fast-growing urban and suburban seats such as Bangi and Damansara.
The 2018 boundaries were not drawn for this electorate. The result is a map in which where you live decides how much your vote is worth.
Why it matters to every Malaysian
Equal voice: every citizen's ballot should carry roughly the same weight. Today, it depends on your postcode.
Fair competition: lopsided boundaries let parties win majorities that do not reflect how people voted and have long-fed suspicion of gerrymandering.
Better service and fairer spending: one MP cannot properly serve 300,000 constituents. Over-represented areas also attract a disproportionate share of political attention and public money.
Trust in elections: a transparent, data-driven review rebuilds confidence in the Election Commission (EC) and gives young and first-time voters a reason to turn out.
The plan: the one-third rule, applied within each state

Section 2(c) of the 13th Schedule of the Federal Constitution already says the number of electors in each constituency within a state ought to be approximately equal while allowing some extra weight for hard-to-reach rural areas.
The plan simply gives that principle a measurable target.

No state gains or loses seats. Perlis keeps three, Pahang keeps 14, Selangor keeps 22. Calculate each state's average number of voters per seat. Redraw the boundaries so every seat falls within one-third (±33%) of that average, aiming for ±25% wherever geography allows. Rural weightage stays, but within a defined limit.
For example, Selangor's 22 parliamentary seats have an average of about 167,000 voters each. Under the one-third rule, each seat would have to have between 111,000 and 222,000 voters.
Shrinking Bangi and enlarging Sabak Bernam – and doing the same across the state – brings every Selangor seat into a defensible range.
Why this is legal and politically passable
Redrawing boundaries inside each state needs only a simple majority to approve the EC's report in the Dewan Rakyat. The 2018 report passed this way.
Changing how many seats each state has would mean amending Article 46, which needs a two-thirds majority (148 of 222 MPs). This plan leaves Article 46 untouched.
The timing is lawful. Article 113 allows a review once eight years have passed since the last one and requires it to finish within two years. The peninsula freeze ended in March 2026.

It has been done this quickly before. The previous peninsula review, begun in 2016, went from start to Dewan Rakyat approval in roughly 18 months. The maths works, the constitution allows it and the timeline is viable. What is missing is the decision to start.
Sabah and Sarawak: complementary, not competing

The federal government has agreed in principle to restore Sabah and Sarawak to one-third of Dewan Rakyat seats, in line with the Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63), and talks with the EC have begun. That is a separate track, as adding seats requires amending Article 46 by a two-thirds majority, plus wide consultation.
The two reforms should run in parallel. Fixing the gaps within each state does not depend on the outcome of the MA63 seat talks – and must not be delayed while those talks continue.
The clock
From now until December, the EC must formally notify the speaker and prime minister. The first proposed maps would then be gazetted and displayed publicly for a month.

From January to March 2027, the first round of local enquiries would hear objections. From April to June 2027, the EC revises maps where justified and puts them up on display for a month if revisions are made.
From July to September 2027, the second round of local enquiries would be held, after which the EC would submit its final report to the prime minister.

From October to November 2027, the report would be tabled at the budget sitting and passed by a simple majority. The royal order could then be made and gazetted before Parliament is dissolved automatically on Dec 19, 2027, if not earlier.
This is tight but achievable, provided the EC begins before the end of 2026 and Parliament is not dissolved before the report is passed.
Answering the critics
“Isn't this too rushed?” The constitution allows two years; this plan uses about 18 months, matching the last peninsula review.
“Who benefits politically?” Voters do and the nation too. Some safe seats will become competitive, which is why incumbents of every party may object.
Call to action
The EC must formally commence the review before the end of 2026.
The prime minister must commit to tabling the final report promptly and to not dissolving Parliament before it is decided.
All MPs and political parties must pledge publicly to support a fair, within-state realignment, regardless of its effect on their own seat.
A fairer map before GE16 is within reach. All it takes is the political will to begin.
(Voter figures are based on the GE15 electoral roll).
Lim Teck Ghee is a public policy analyst.
